text:
Dow Inc. DOW recently launched VOLTRICELL, a new battery cell materials platform designed to optimize battery manufacturing and improve performance. The platform expands Dow's battery solutions portfolio and strengthens its presence in the industry.

Dow, which is among the leading companies in the chemical space, along with DuPont de Nemours, Inc. DD, Eastman Chemical Company EMN and Air Products and Chemicals, Inc. APD, aims to bring together materials for electrodes, separators, coatings and battery cell packaging, including binders, dispersants, rheology modifiers, surfactants and specialty additives, through VOLTRICELL. These materials are designed to support higher energy density, longer cycle life, faster charging and scalable manufacturing. The platform integrates emerging technologies such as sodium-ion, silicon-anode and solid-state batteries.

The new launch will be complemented by VORAFORCE TP1415 polyurethane resin for lightweight, flame-retardant composites, DOWSIL EF-6559 silicone foam for thermal management and electrical insulation, and DOWSIL FC-2024 coating for protecting battery housings and enclosures during thermal events.

The introduction of VOLTRICELL supports growth by addressing manufacturers' demand for materials that improve battery performance, safety and production scalability across the battery value chain. It builds on its deep materials science expertise and application development capabilities to foster innovation.

For the second half of 2026, management plans to focus on growth and innovation in attractive end markets, investments to strengthen the portfolio and balanced capital allocation. Dow expects the growth and productivity benefits from Transform to Outperform to accelerate through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027. Dow expects approximately $200 million in additional benefits from Transform to Outperform during 2026. This raises the company's expected total in-year benefits from self-help initiatives to more than $1.3 billion.

Another industry leader, DuPont, raised the midpoint of its full-year 2026 operating EBITDA and adjusted earnings guidance. The company now expects net sales in the range of $7.16-$7.19 billion, operating EBITDA between $1.75 billion and $1.77 billion and adjusted earnings of $7.17-$7.32 per share. The outlook reflects continued strength across healthcare, industrial water and aerospace end markets. Management expects mid-single-digit organic sales growth in the second half and remains focused on productivity, profitable growth and shareholder value creation.

Eastman, on its second-quarter call, said that it expects earnings to improve significantly from 2025. The company remains on track to deliver cost reductions of $125 million to $150 million, net of inflation. For the third quarter, adjusted earnings are projected to approach the second-quarter level of $1.97 per share. Advanced Materials EBIT is expected to increase on improved price-cost and asset utilization, while Fibers earnings should benefit from higher acetate tow purchases. Additives & Functional Products earnings are expected to decline modestly due to seasonal agriculture weakness, while Chemical Intermediates earnings are projected to ease as supply-chain disruptions lessen.

Air Products, for fiscal 2026, raised its adjusted earnings guidance to $13.39-$13.49 per share from the prior range of $13-$13.25. For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Air Products expects adjusted earnings of $3.55-$3.65 per share. The company now anticipates fiscal 2026 capital expenditures of approximately $3.5 billion, below its earlier projection of about $4 billion. Management expects new asset contributions, pricing actions and productivity initiatives to support performance, while remaining cautious because of macroeconomic uncertainty.

text:
HedgeCo.Net — The Bank of England is examining whether Barclays traders misrepresented illiquid private credit loans in a way that understated their risk, the Financial Times reported on Monday, October 19, citing people familiar with the matter. Reuters and Investing.com both carried the report. The central bank’s Prudential Regulation Authority received a complaint from an insider earlier this year about how Barclays recorded derivatives used to finance private credit loans.

According to the FT, as relayed by Reuters, the complaint centers on total return swaps referencing illiquid private credit loans that Barclays allocated to its trading book rather than its banking book. Total return swaps let banks finance loans for private credit funds while passing the economic performance of those loans to clients for a fee. Barclays traders argued the exposure could be treated as a traded position because it was hedged through a matching swap with another counterparty, the report said. The FT did not disclose the size of the positions.

The classification matters because it drives capital. The concern is that booking derivatives tied to illiquid loans as easier-to-trade instruments can understate the underlying risk and reduce the capital a bank must hold against losses. The complaint also alleged the treatment breached PRA rules that restrict banks from putting derivatives backed by illiquid collateral in the trading book without sufficient evidence to justify it. The Bank of England declined to comment, and Barclays said it takes its regulatory obligations seriously but would not discuss its interactions with regulators.

Barclays shares fell 2.6% to 421.4 pence in early London trading, Reuters reported, while the FTSE 100 was down 0.9%. For private credit managers, the story is less about one bank than about the plumbing behind fund-level leverage. Bank financing lines, including swap-based structures, sit underneath many direct-lending and asset-based strategies, and any supervisory push to reprice or reclassify that financing could raise the cost of leverage for funds.

The examination comes amid growing regulatory attention on the roughly $2 trillion private credit market. Investors will watch whether the PRA broadens its review to other lenders’ swap books, and whether banks respond by tightening terms on financing provided to private credit vehicles.

text:
Highlights

AI-powered study tools gaining traction.

New AI lab certification agreement.

Full-year guidance reiterated.

Pearson, the global learning company, is positioning itself as a key beneficiary of AI-driven reskilling.This update falls within our AI Stocks coverage.

Pearson's AI Strategy

Pearson (LSE:PSON) Communication Services Pearson PLC (LSE:PSON) 1374.50 GBX +21.500 ↑ 1.589% provides educational content, assessments, digital learning tools and professional qualifications. Its businesses include Assessment and Qualifications, Virtual Learning, Higher Education, English Language Learning and Enterprise Learning and Skills. It is a constituent of the FTSE 100.

AI stocks include not only technology developers but also companies using AI to transform their products. Pearson is embedding AI across its learning tools and helping businesses train employees for an AI-driven economy.

First-Half Results

In the first half of 2026, Pearson reported underlying revenue growth in line with expectations and a strong increase in adjusted operating profit. Operating cash flow and free cash flow improved significantly.

Virtual Learning delivered the strongest growth, supported by enrolment momentum, while Enterprise Learning and Skills grew on vocational qualifications and enterprise solutions. Assessment and Qualifications returned to growth in the second quarter, though English Language Learning declined.

Guidance Reiterated

Pearson reiterated its full-year guidance for steady underlying revenue growth and adjusted operating profit within its target range, with growth expected to improve in the second half, particularly in the third quarter.

AI Products and Partnerships

Pearson's AI-powered study tools in Higher Education have shown strong results, with research suggesting students using its adaptive products are far more likely to reach initial mastery of a topic than with legacy tools.

In Enterprise, Pearson signed a new agreement with a leading AI lab to deliver its global certification programme and expanded strategic accounts through a partnership with Adobe. It also delivers AI fluency programmes for corporate clients.

AI Skills Verification

As AI changes the workplace, employers need ways to verify employee skills. Pearson's assessment expertise positions it to offer trusted certification for AI skills, a growing market.

The Reskilling Opportunity

AI is changing the skills employers need, creating demand for training and certification. Companies are investing in programmes to help employees use AI tools effectively, and individuals are seeking qualifications to stay competitive. Pearson's combination of content, assessment and technology makes it well placed to serve this demand.

Partnerships with technology companies and AI labs help Pearson develop relevant programmes and reach large numbers of learners.

Virtual Learning

Pearson's Virtual Learning business runs online schools and provides technology for virtual education. Strong enrolment growth has made it one of the company's fastest-growing divisions.

What Sets It Apart

Pearson's trusted brand, large content library, assessment expertise and relationships with educational institutions and employers give it advantages over newer AI education start-ups. Its data on learning outcomes helps improve its AI tools.

What Investors Are Watching

Investors will look for evidence of faster growth in the third quarter, particularly in Higher Education and Virtual Learning, along with progress on enterprise AI partnerships. Any update on English language testing trends will also be important, as this business has been under pressure.

The Wider Market Backdrop

Information and education companies have faced questions about AI disruption in 2026. Pearson's ability to show AI-driven growth has helped differentiate it, though shares remain sensitive to sentiment about the sector.

For AI investors, Pearson offers exposure to AI adoption in education and workforce training.

Risks for AI Investors

Risks include competition from AI-native learning platforms, pressure on English language testing, changes in education funding, currency movements and execution of its AI strategy.

Key Takeaways for Readers

Pearson is using AI to strengthen its learning products and tap demand for reskilling. Its enterprise partnerships highlight new growth opportunities.

Readers should watch Virtual Learning and Enterprise growth, as these are the main drivers of the company's improving outlook.

For readers comparing AI stocks, Pearson offers exposure to AI adoption rather than AI infrastructure. What drives a company's dividend

A company's dividend usually reflects its profits, cash flow and the board's view of how much it needs to keep for investment, debt repayment or acquisitions. Boards can raise, hold, cut or suspend payments as trading conditions change, and decisions are normally announced alongside results. Looking at the trend in earnings and cash generation over several periods often says more about the reliability of a dividend than any single payment.

text:
Banco Santander today announced a new milestone in their artificial intelligence collaboration with NVIDIA. With support from NVIDIA, the Santander AI Lab has developed new capabilities to evaluate AI models and agents for banking applications, helping identify which model is best suited for each task and deploy it in the most efficient way.

The work is being carried out through Santander AI Lab, which explores and tests emerging AI technologies before broader deployment across the bank. As part of this effort, Santander has been progressively moving from large general-purpose models towards smaller, specialised models designed for specific banking tasks. In selected experimental use cases, this approach has reduced serving costs from around €5 per interaction to approximately €0.03 while maintaining strong performance.

Through the Lab, Santander has built Model Arena to evaluate open-weight models against banking tasks and identify the right model for each workload, and is specialising models using NVIDIA NeMo Customizer. Customer-service comparisons delivered evidence that smaller, specialised models can deliver strong performance on targeted banking tasks. Santander has built specialised intelligence for core banking workloads on NVIDIA Kumo, a family of open-weight foundation models for structured data, allowing companies to quickly turn structured data into predictive insights needed for agentic services.

The Lab is industrialising inference within Santander’s own architecture using NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton, the approach behind the serving-cost reduction above, and is developing Model Arena to design, simulate, evaluate and supervise banking agents, alongside performance engineering and adversarial testing of conversational AI in controlled environments. The goal is to establish a rigorous experimentation path through which emerging AI technologies are optimised and stress-tested against banking requirements before successful capabilities scale across Santander.

Building on these advances, Santander is progressing from open-weight models towards specialised models and governed banking agents designed for greater control, safety and lower operating costs at scale. The collaboration is already delivering measurable results: in an experimental customer-service use case, Santander improved conversation quality while reducing costs by more than 50% through the deployment of a more efficient AI model.

As part of the next phase of the initiative, Santander and NVIDIA have established a three-year collaboration framework covering areas such as foundation models, AI agents, fraud and anti-money laundering capabilities, real-time decisioning and advanced simulation technologies, including a banking digital twin.

"NVIDIA is a key player in the infrastructure, software and research that is powering the latest advances in artificial intelligence. Combined with Santander's scale across businesses, customers and geographies, we believe we are uniquely positioned to succeed in transforming those advances into practical banking capabilities." said Iñaki Bernal, chief artificial intelligence officer at Santander.

"Banking is one of the most data-centric industries. Data sits at the heart of every process and now banks need to become intelligence-centric. Transforming years of data into usable and proprietary intelligence is not about model size, but about training and fine tuning. In this new world, cost per intelligence output is a key metric. Santander is showing what that looks like in production with smaller models, specialised on the bank’s own data, evaluated against real banking tasks and served efficiently enough to run at the scale of a global bank." said Aser Blanco, Global Banking Lead at NVIDIA.

text:
Microsoft has pulled out of plans to build the UK’s largest AI data centre in a deal with Nscale.

The global tech giant, which had previously planned to fund a supercomputer at the site, has ended its involvement in the partnership following concerns over supply issues.

Plans were first announced last year, with Nscale pledging £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton, Essex. The government hailed the agreement at the time with former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer highlighting the project in the UK’s AI strategy in 2025.

But Microsoft, which was being viewed as the anchor tenant for the centre, has pulled the plug on its end of the deal after UK Power Networks said the power connection for the site would not be available for its 2026 target due to upstream grid capacity issues.

“We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK,” an Nscale spokesperson said following news of Microsoft’s withdrawal, which was first reported by The Telegraph.

“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”

The two firms are engaged in tie-ups across Europe and the United States.

Nscale heading for blockbuster listing

Nscale, which was founded in London, is backed by global tech giants including Nvidia and has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” datacentre.

The loss of Microsoft on the Loughton project hands a timely blow to the firm as it gears up for a blockbuster listing in New York.

It is planning to list on the New York Stock Exchange – with a target valuation of reportedly up to $35bn – while maintaining its British domicile.

The London-based firm, which has former deputy prime minister Nick Clegg and former Meta executive Sheryl Sandberg as members of its board, reported a net of loss of $1bn on revenues of $141m in the first half of the year, with the bulk of losses caused by non-cash charges.

In March the group was valued at roughly $14.6bn in a funding round led by Norwegian energy group Aker and 8090 industries. Nvidia, Dell and Nokia also participated in the round.

A Microsoft spokesperson said: “We remain committed to our partnership with Nscale, including work to build robust digital infrastructure and support AI growth globally. This decision relates to a single site.”

As a result, it is also proposing to designate Microsoft as having strategic market status (SMS) in the UK’s business software market.

text:
The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has revealed Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft have made progress in addressing barriers to competition in cloud services, but more needs to be done to give businesses greater choice.

The watchdog said it is continuing discussions with both companies to secure further improvements. As a result, it is also proposing to designate Microsoft as having strategic market status (SMS) in the UK’s business software market.

According to the company, the proposed designation could pave the way for closer scrutiny of Microsoft’s business practices, including how it bundles products, integrates services and licenses software for use on rival cloud platforms.

However, the CMA will consult on the proposal before making a final decision.

According to the regulator, Microsoft holds a strong position across five key areas: PC operating systems, productivity software, security software, server operating systems and database management systems.

The CMA said customers face difficulties switching providers, while Microsoft’s commercial practices and the way its products work together can make it harder for competing software developers to attract users. As part of its proposed next steps, the watchdog will examine whether businesses have enough freedom to choose where they run their software, particularly when using cloud services from competing providers.

It will also assess whether Microsoft’s software licensing arrangements discourage customers from using alternative cloud platforms.

Another area of concern is artificial intelligence, with the CMA looking at whether businesses can freely choose AI tools from different suppliers or face barriers when using alternatives to Microsoft’s Copilot.

CMA CEO, Sarah Cardell, said: “Business software and cloud services underpin workplaces across the UK, from small firms to vital public services. The evidence shows Microsoft has a long-standing and significant presence in the UK’s business software market.

“Organisations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers. We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft’s products alongside alternatives.

“We’re now consulting on whether to designate Microsoft with strategic market status. If we do, our focus would be on promoting competition and giving businesses greater freedom to choose and combine products in business software.”

She added: “We’ve also been engaging with AWS and Microsoft outside a formal designation process to deliver greater customer choice in cloud services. Meaningful improvements have already been made, with more to come and we’re continuing to work with both companies to agree further actions.”

Meanwhile an Amazon spokesperson continued: “We welcome the outcome of the Competition and Markets Authority’s (CMA) review, which recognises the concrete steps AWS has taken to enhance customer choice and flexibility in the UK.

“As outlined in our recent blog, we’ve continued to invest throughout 2026 in new AI, multi-cloud, and open-standard capabilities that give customers more control over how they build and operate, to help the UK’s innovation economy thrive.”

title: These 3 Green Stocks Have a Growth Story That Goes Far Beyond Washington
description:
A 2026 London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) report found that since 2008, the green economy has outperformed global equities by 133%.
As a standalone sector, the green economy would rank as the third-largest industry, behind only technology and industrials.
But the best green stocks don't need that outcome.
The Water Play Behind AI Ecolab ECL doesn't look like a green growth stock.

text:
Green stocks have a reputation problem. Many investors still treat them as policy trades that rise and fall with Washington. The data tells a different story.

A 2026 London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) report found that since 2008, the green economy has outperformed global equities by 133%. LSEG defines it as companies selling products and services with environmental benefits. Their combined market capitalization topped $10 trillion for the first time in Q4 2025.

As a standalone sector, the green economy would rank as the third-largest industry, behind only technology and industrials. And green equities beat the broader market by 12.4% over the past 12 months.

That happened even as the Trump administration shifted federal priorities toward domestic oil and gas production. It suggests demand is coming from economics, not subsidies.

November's midterms could add upside if a Democratic wave revives climate policy. But the best green stocks don't need that outcome. Here are three companies growing on commercial demand that would gain further from any policy tailwind.

Selling Speed to Power-Hungry Data Centers

Bloom Energy BE makes solid-oxide fuel cells that generate electricity on-site. In a world where the existing electric grid can't keep up, demand is surging.

The AI infrastructure story adds to but isn't the entire thesis. Grid interconnection queues have become the binding constraint on data-center buildouts, and Bloom sells the workaround. That's a commercial problem with a commercial solution.

In Q2 2026, revenue hit a record $1.065 billion, the company's first quarter above $1 billion, up 166% year over year. Earnings per share (EPS) of 78 cents beat the consensus estimate of 39 cents. Management also raised full-year revenue guidance to $3.9 billion to $4.2 billion.

The company says all the major U.S. hyperscalers have validated and approved its power solutions for their AI factories. It also signed a 2.8-gigawatt agreement with Oracle ORCL in April 2026.

One caveat for investors is valuation. BE shares are up nearly 160% in 2026 and trade near 112x forward earnings. Because of its importance to the data center buildout, investors should expect volatility around the company's Q3 earnings report, confirmed for Oct. 22.

Bloom's systems mostly run on natural gas today, which purists will note. But they can also run on biogas and hydrogen. Richer clean energy credits would sweeten project economics. That's upside that may not be reflected in the current forecasts.

The Water Play Behind AI

Ecolab ECL doesn't look like a green growth stock. It's a century-old water and hygiene company. But water efficiency is becoming one of the most valuable services in the AI buildout.

Data centers and chip fabs consume enormous amounts of water. Ecolab helps them use less. Global High-Tech sales rose 29% in the second quarter on demand from data centers and AI infrastructure.

The July acquisition of liquid-cooling provider CoolIT Systems deepens that exposure. The platform is nearing $1.5 billion in annualized sales, and management targets 25%+ annual growth to reach $4 billion by 2030.

The core business is steadier. Second-quarter EPS of $2.09 edged past estimates, and revenue rose 9.7% year over year. Management raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $8.05 to $8.25.

The sweet spot for investors is that this growth comes with defensive characteristics. Ecolab has raised its dividend for 33 years. Analysts rate ECL as a Moderate Buy with a $324.50 consensus target.

The stock isn't cheap at about 35x forward earnings. But its growth comes from customers cutting costs, not from regulators.

Holding Up Without Washington’s Help

Brookfield Renewable Partners BEP is the clearest test of this thesis. It owns hydro, wind, solar, and storage assets and has direct exposure to renewable tax policy. Despite that, BEP is up over 5% this year.

The business explains the bull case. Second-quarter funds from operations (FFO) hit a record 62 cents per unit, up 11% year over year. The company remains on track to deliver about 10,000 megawatts of new projects per year by 2027.

Much of that demand comes from Big Tech. Brookfield has a framework agreement to deliver more than 10,500 megawatts of renewable capacity to Microsoft MSFT, plus a deal with Alphabet GOOGL for up to 3,000 megawatts of hydro. These deals aren't about tax incentives. Hyperscalers are signing these deals because they need reliable, around-the-clock power.

Analysts see more room to run. BEP carries a Moderate Buy consensus rating with a $37.43 price target implying about 30% upside from recent trading levels. The dividend yields roughly 5.5% and trades at about 0.25 times book value.

One structural note. Brookfield is converting BEP and its sister security, Brookfield Renewable Corp. BEPC, into a single corporation. BEP units will be exchanged one-for-one for shares of the new BEP Inc.

Of the three, Brookfield has the most direct exposure to renewable tax policy. A pro-climate Congress would be a meaningful tailwind. Its growth so far hasn’t needed one.

Buy the Demand, Treat Policy as a Bonus

The LSEG data reminds investors of an important point that matters in every sector. Green companies win when they save customers money or solve urgent problems. Policy helps, but it isn't the engine. Each of these companies would benefit from a Democratic wave in November, but none depends on one.

Andrea Orcel-led Italian banking giant UniCredit has received authorisation from the European Central Bank (ECB) to take control of Commerzbank.

The ECB authorisation is a major regulatory win for UniCredit, that tirelessly pursued the Commerzbank’s acquisition, after investing in its German counterpart in September 2024.

Despite putting on fierce resistance to UniCredit’s M&A effort, Commerzbank and the German government had to eventually concede in July 2026, as the Italian lender muscled up its stake in its acquisition target close to 48%.

UniCredit needed ECB approval to take delivery of the Commerzbank shares tendered in the 45 billion euro (USD 50.51 billion) offer and advance plans for ⁠what would be Europe’s biggest cross-border banking deal since the global financial crisis.

UniCredit said the ECB had authorised it to cross the 30% ownership threshold in Commerzbank and “to increase its stake further without upper limits.”

It added that it expected to be able to take control of Commerzbank by the end of the year with around 50% of voting rights after completing the “remaining regulatory processes and conditions” relating to its takeover bid.

The Italian bank, which has operated Bavarian lender HVB in Germany since 2005, always had Commerzbank in its acquisition radar, with several of Orcel’s predecessors studying the prospect.

Despite stiff opposition from Commerzbank and criticism from the German government, UniCredit secured enough shares to control ordinary shareholder resolutions while remaining below the 50% threshold that would force it to buy ⁠out minority investors in the German lender’s Polish unit, mBank.

Orcel has told Commerzbank to adopt the strategy he has mapped out to boost profits at the Frankfurt-based bank from January, while pushing back a full ⁠merger to 2029-2030.

The veteran dealmaker has held talks with German government representatives who want Commerzbank to retain its Frankfurt headquarters, to protect jobs and to lend to German businesses.

Yu's argument is not simply that Chinese labs could catch up. It is that many customers may not need the extra capability in the first place.

Cost matters beyond choosing between models. Yu said executives he works with also weigh spending on AI tokens against simply hiring more people.

Yu said enterprises are already using Chinese open models, including a well-known Andreessen Horowitz-backed Silicon Valley startup.

Intel Corp. CEO Lip-Bu Tan made a similar point this week, saying models including DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM were already "good enough," with lower token costs and "very fast" adoption.

Yu does not expect that pressure to dislodge OpenAI or Anthropic as easily in the Western consumer market.

text:
Volvo Cars and Mercedes-Benz have both expanded their partnerships with NVIDIA to develop automated driving for future vehicles, with the two carmakers set to use the same core NVIDIA software and hardware.

In separate announcements made on 15 and 16 October, NVIDIA said Volvo will use its Hyperion sensor and computing architecture, Alpamayo Stack driving software and Halos safety system. Mercedes-Benz will combine the same three NVIDIA products with its own MB.OS vehicle operating system.

Volvo said the system is designed to drive "door to door", covering highways, busy city streets and parking.

The companies plan to introduce eyes-off driving first, followed by mind-off driving, in which the driver would no longer need to supervise the car.

The technology will first appear in a next-generation Volvo that forms part of what the company describes as its largest-ever product programme. Volvo has not named the model or given a launch date.

The two companies have worked together since 2017. Håkan Samuelsson, president and CEO of Volvo Cars, said: "Volvo has been synonymous with car safety for almost 100 years."

He said pairing that experience with NVIDIA's AI technology would enable Volvo to build safer, more attractive cars.

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang said accelerated computing had turned the car into "an intelligent machine that can understand the world around it".

Volvo's safety record has recently been tested on the battery side. An EV Infrastructure News analysis of EV fire statistics lists Volvo's 2025 recall of 40,000 EX30 models worldwide, 10,500 of them in the UK, among recalls linked to battery fire risk.

Volvo sold more than 710,000 cars in 2025, 46% of them electrified, according to the company.

Mercedes-Benz targets Level 4

NVIDIA said its extended partnership with Mercedes-Benz covers the next generation of driver assistance and automated driving, including future SAE Level 4 applications such as robolimousines. Level 4 systems can drive without human supervision in defined conditions.

Within that setup, Alpamayo provides AI-based driving software for point-to-point urban assistance, active safety and automated parking, according to NVIDIA. Halos operates as a parallel safety system, adding redundancy.

Jörg Burzer, chief technology officer and board member at Mercedes-Benz Group, said: "NVIDIA is our most important strategic partner in automated driving."

He said the two companies had jointly developed the first Mercedes-Benz assistance system for urban point-to-point driving in the western world.

Mercedes-Benz also uses NVIDIA technology for engineering simulation and in MO360, its digital production platform.

Neither company disclosed financial terms or a timeline for the expanded work. Mercedes-Benz sold more than 2.1 million passenger cars and vans in 2025.

The NVIDIA deal adds to other recent supply and service agreements at Mercedes-Benz. In April, Samsung SDI agreed to supply high-nickel batteries for the carmaker's compact and mid-size electric SUVs and coupes, the battery maker's first deal with Mercedes-Benz.

In August, Mercedes-Benz and ChargePoint launched a fleet charging service for business customers in the UK and Germany, covering site planning, installation, operation and maintenance.

text:
Artificial intelligence and big data have overtaken climate change as the risk that experts worldwide are most worried about, driven by growing concern over side effects such as the misuse of personal data and human rights violations as AI spreads rapidly.

Experts around the world named "AI and big data" as the risk likely to have the greatest impact over the next five to 10 years, according to the 2026 AXA Future Risks Report, published on the 19th by AXA Group with global market research firm Ipsos. The risk climbed three places from fourth last year, displacing climate change for the first time after it had ranked first for seven consecutive years. Among the general public, AI and big data jumped to second this year from seventh a year earlier.

The survey polled 4,345 insurance experts in 62 countries and 24,000 members of the general public in 19 countries. After AI and big data, experts cited climate change, geopolitical instability, cybersecurity and the energy crisis as the top future risks. The general public ranked climate change as the biggest risk.

Ethical issues drew the greatest concern regarding AI. Some 34% of both experts and general-public respondents pointed to human rights violations, data misuse and bias as major risks. The impact on the job market and the "black box effect," in which AI decision-making cannot easily be explained, were also raised. Among experts who selected AI-related risks as a major concern, 54% said the risks were growing quickly, but only 9% said governments and regulators were sufficiently prepared.

Korean experts also named AI and big data as the biggest future risk. Cybersecurity, which ranked fourth in the global expert survey, came in second in Korea. The gap suggests relatively heightened wariness in Korea about security threats in the digital environment, including ransomware, personal data leaks and extortion.

AXA Group also stressed the importance of prevention in responding to emerging risks. Some 85% of experts and members of the general public said major risks could be at least partly reduced through preventive measures. Among the general public, 68% said insurers play an important role in protecting society from new risks.

"The risk environment is becoming more complex, with AI, cyber threats and climate change," said Hans Branken, chief executive of AXA General Insurance. "Based on research and analysis of global risks, we will strengthen prevention-focused protection for our customers."

text:
Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA announced that they will extend their strategic partnership to advance the next generation of automated driving systems.

The collaboration brings together Mercedes-Benz’s automotive engineering and safety expertise and its MB.OS operating system with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI technologies.

Mercedes-Benz’s MB.OS operating system supports new driving functions and over-the-air updates, working with NVIDIA Hyperion’s in-vehicle computing and sensor architecture. NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack provides full-stack driving software with AI reasoning capabilities, supporting point-to-point urban assistance, active safety and automated parking. NVIDIA Halos adds to the Mercedes-Benz safety foundation, including a parallel safety stack that adds redundancy and guardrails. Together, these technologies support advanced driver assistance and the development of future SAE-Level 4 applications, including robolimousines.

Beyond automated driving, Mercedes-Benz also relies on NVIDIA technologies for vehicle engineering simulation and within MO360, its digital production ecosystem — from virtual planning to AI-based applications. The two partners are working to further enhance efficiency, flexibility and quality across the global production network.

Jörg Burzer, Member of the Board of Management of Mercedes-Benz Group AG and Chief Technology Officer, Development and Procurement:

NVIDIA is our most important strategic partner in automated driving. Together, we developed the first Mercedes-Benz assistance system for urban point-to-point driving for the western world. The expansion of our partnership marks a significant milestone and reflects the mutual trust we have built over the years. Together, we aim to bring further pioneering innovations to the road, offering our customers the best automated driving experience while upholding the high safety standards they expect from a Mercedes-Benz.

Ali Kani, Vice President of Automotive at NVIDIA:

Accelerated computing is giving vehicles the intelligence to understand the world and reason through complex driving situations. Mercedes-Benz brings the engineering excellence and commitment to safety this transformation demands. Together, we’re building on NVIDIA Hyperion to bring that intelligence and full-stack safety to the road and make autonomous driving an everyday reality.

title: The next AI race will be won at the credit desk - Fortune
description:
The next phase of the AI race between companies and countries will depend in large part on who can pay for it; the action is shifting from frontier labs to credit desks.
Whoever can raise capital cheaply and at scale will set the pace, and that race still favors the United States, whose capital markets are deeper than anyone else’s.
The five largest American hyperscalers alone are on track to spend $730 billion on capital expenditure in 2026.
In contrast, graphics processing units (GPUs) are short-lived assets; AI demand is unpredictable; and it is too early to project returns.
The capital comes from third parties: pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, household savings.
text:
It also points to the wider direction of travel in AI. Even as the world obsesses about model releases, chip capabilities, and data center capacity, the variable that increasingly determines who gets to compete is simply money. The next phase of the AI race between companies and countries will depend in large part on who can pay for it; the action is shifting from frontier labs to credit desks. Whoever can raise capital cheaply and at scale will set the pace, and that race still favors the United States, whose capital markets are deeper than anyone else’s. For China and Europe, the road to closing the technological gap runs through the financial one.

Technological revolutions tend to be remembered for their technologies: steam engines, railways, the internet. Just as important is the financial machinery that made them possible: the joint-stock company dispersed the risk of trading voyages; early bond and equity markets financed railroads before they could produce a return; venture capital supplied high-risk money to companies too new to raise it from traditional investors.

AI is reaching its own version of this moment. For half a century, technology was asset-light: software could be written once and distributed to billions at negligible marginal cost. AI is turning technology into a heavy industry. The latest systems require factories, advanced chips, substations, and enormous supplies of electricity. Even the world’s richest companies are finding it hard to fund all of this from their income.

The five largest American hyperscalers alone are on track to spend $730 billion on capital expenditure in 2026. A shrinking proportion is coming from their own balance sheets; they are expected to finance up to a third of it with debt.

If the most profitable companies in history have to borrow to stay in the race, what hope is there for everyone else?

Nvidia’s deal is one answer. Project finance has long funded infrastructure with high up-front costs, paid down by steady returns over many years: power plants, toll roads, airports. What’s new is the attempt to turn compute into an asset class that pension funds and insurers are comfortable owning, the way they already own infrastructure.

The arrangement carries risks. The parallel with infrastructure is imperfect: Energy facilities are built to last decades, usually in response to foreseeable demand, and generate predictable returns. In contrast, graphics processing units (GPUs) are short-lived assets; AI demand is unpredictable; and it is too early to project returns.

Still, if the upsides from AI are speculative, so are the downsides—and if the model works, it could reshape the AI market much as venture capital changed the risk calculus for starting a business.

Nvidia’s announcement came with familiar worries about circular financing, in which the chipmaker’s money comes back to it as chip orders. But this arrangement is the opposite. Nvidia will not, for the most part, be lending its own money—nor will its six partners. The capital comes from third parties: pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, household savings. Rather than a closed loop, the buildout is being wired into the wider financial system: the deal does not artificially boost demand but restructures the cost of supply for a wider bench of competitors beyond the hyperscalers, who can themselves only partially afford it.

Financial structure will in part pick the winners of the technology race—not by who has more money, but by whether the wider financial architecture puts capital to optimal use.

Europe illustrates the problem. The continent has one of the world’s largest pools of savings; eurozone households alone hold about 10 trillion euros (about $11 trillion) in bank deposits. Yet European institutional investors would rather buy U.S. tech bonds than back their own startups. The money is there; what’s missing is the plumbing to turn savings into investment.

If AI comes down to access to capital, Europe’s AI strategy needs a capital-markets strategy—and progress on long-stalled capital-markets integration would do more for European competitiveness than another round of gigafactories.

China’s problem runs the other way. State money is good at pouring concrete; it is less good at matching capacity to demand: after a policy-driven building spree, Chinese media reported last year that as much as 80% of newly built computing capacity sat unused. The Stanford HAI AI Index 2026 estimates that last year, private investment in AI in the U.S. was more than 23 times that in China.

With finance picking the winners, the United States starts with an edge: No other country is as good at turning the savings of pensioners and households into risky, long-lived assets at scale. America’s bond markets, private credit funds, and asset managers are already looking for exactly this kind of asset—how else could a chipmaker line up a half-trillion-dollar financing target in a single announcement?

The first phase of the AI boom relied on technical breakthroughs: models, chips, applications. The next phase depends on the financial system’s ability to underwrite the industry’s expansion beyond a small set of companies. Nvidia has made a bold attempt to reconfigure the economics of AI; competitors will need equally imaginative financial machinery of their own.

Technological revolutions do not happen simply because someone invents the future. They happen when they also figure out how to pay for it.

description:

NVHBM, unveiled in August, integrates Nvidia’s custom memory controller into the base die and is aimed at standardising implementation across multiple memory suppliers, said the company.

It is also assessing whether its foundry could produce NVHBM base dies if demand exceeds TSMC’s capacity, the newspaper quoted an unnamed source as saying.

text:
Amazon, Yelp, Delta Air Lines, JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have all moved to shut third-party AI agents out of the parts of their sites where real tasks get done, The Verge reported on October 17.

The failures piled up on users of Meta's Muse, xAI's Grok, and OpenAI's Dots and Instinct in recent days.

Amazon began blocking Muse on September 20, roughly 12 days after Meta launched the shopping agent, after Meta declined Amazon's request to remove it. Amazon told reporters that Meta had not disclosed Muse would access the retail site and that the agent did not identify itself as AI while browsing. Yelp will admit only agents enrolled in its paid data-licensing program; Delta says it has no deals with third-party agents; JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab say the agents cannot touch customer accounts.

The banks frame it as a credentials problem. "We don't want someone just giving their password to Muse, and letting Muse come in and take action on that client's behalf," Charles Schwab chief executive Rick Wurster said. Bank of America chief executive Brian Moynihan has signaled his bank will require human authorization for payments until agents prove more reliable.

Meta's position is that the blocks hurt the customer, not just the agent. "Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it," the company said, and insisted Muse "cannot see passwords or payment methods." It pointed to live integrations with Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, Sephora and Wayfair, plus a Shopify default that enables Meta checkout for eligible stores.

text:
The sale of Toggenburg Mountain, near Syracuse, was announced Friday by the New York attorney general’s office, according to an Oct. 16 report by Matthew Perlman in Law360. The buyer intends to reopen the mountain, potentially restoring a skiing option that disappeared after Intermountain acquired the property.

The transaction follows a lawsuit filed in 2022 accusing Intermountain of reducing competition by purchasing and closing a rival ski operation. State regulators argued that the acquisition strengthened the company’s control over the regional market for ski season passes, limiting consumer choice.

Buyer Plans to Restore Ski Operations

Local businessman Douglas Wheeler purchased Toggenburg under a settlement negotiated with New York Attorney General Letitia James. Wheeler plans to renovate the property and resume skiing operations during the 2027-28 winter season, according to the attorney general’s Oct. 16 announcement.

The agreement also requires Intermountain to pay $30,000 to New York state. For four years, the company is barred from attempting to buy back Toggenburg or enforcing an employee-recruitment restriction associated with the earlier acquisition.

The settlement addresses a dispute that began in 2021, when Intermountain, already the operator of Song Mountain and Labrador Mountain, purchased Toggenburg and promptly closed it.

According to the attorney general’s office, Intermountain also secured a five-year agreement preventing Toggenburg’s former owners from operating competing businesses within 30 miles. The arrangement included restrictions on recruiting Intermountain employees.

State officials said the closure left Intermountain as the sole operator in the Syracuse-area ski market, contributing to increased prices and congestion at the remaining resorts.

Court Ruling Strengthened State’s Case

The legal proceedings reached a turning point in March 2025, when a New York state judge ruled that Intermountain had violated state antitrust law through its acquisition and closure of Toggenburg and associated restrictions on competition.

The ruling gave the attorney general’s office a stronger position in seeking a sale that would return the property to its previous use.

Read more: Vail Resorts Directors Face Shareholder Suit Over Alleged Ski-Pricing Antitrust Failures

Intermountain had pursued a different outcome, seeking approval to sell the mountain for residential development rather than restore skiing operations, according to the attorney general’s office.

The settlement ultimately secured a buyer committed to reopening the facility.

Competition and Consumer Impact

The dispute highlights how state antitrust enforcement can extend beyond large corporate mergers to acquisitions affecting relatively small regional markets.

For regulators, the central concern was not simply Intermountain’s ownership of multiple resorts, but the removal of a competing business that had previously offered consumers an alternative.

In a statement announcing the settlement, James said restoring competition would benefit skiers through greater choice and potentially improved pricing and service.

The attorney general characterized the transaction as a remedy for market concentration that had harmed consumers and restricted employment opportunities.

The sale does not immediately restore competition, however. Toggenburg remains closed, and its return depends on the completion of Wheeler’s planned improvements.

The new owner’s family has longstanding ties to the property. According to Spectrum News, the Wheeler family previously owned the land on which the resort was developed and intends to modernize the facility while preserving its identity as a local skiing destination.

The transaction closes a significant chapter in New York’s enforcement action against Intermountain while leaving the practical task of reviving the mountain to its new owner.

text:
What’s in This Article

The Announcement Gap Is Becoming a Financing Issue

Nvidia Established the Model

Chart 1. How Circular AI Financing Converts Support Into Supplier Demand

Broadcom, Oracle and SpaceX Extend the Model

The Financial Commitments Behind AI Infrastructure

Table 1. Selected AI Infrastructure Financing Arrangements and Commitments, 2026

Circular Financing and the Expanding Role of Institutional Capital

OpenAI’s Revenue Discrepancy Exposes the Financing Question

Investor Takeaway

The Announcement Gap Is Becoming a Financing Issue

Artificial intelligence infrastructure spending is entering a new phase in which the ability to finance semiconductor purchases is becoming nearly as important as the performance of the processors themselves. Nvidia (NVDA), which established its dominance through graphics processing units, networking technology and its CUDA software ecosystem, is increasingly using financial relationships to reinforce its competitive position. However, Broadcom (AVGO), Oracle (ORCL) and SpaceX are now pursuing financing arrangements involving tens of billions of dollars, suggesting that access to capital could become an increasingly important determinant of market share in AI computing.

In my July 30 Substack analysis, “The Announcement Gap,” I examined how circular financing was becoming an increasingly important feature of the artificial intelligence industry. Nvidia was investing in companies that were simultaneously purchasing its processors, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) was offering equity warrants tied to customer GPU deployments. The concern was not whether semiconductor demand was real, but whether the financing supporting that demand was independent of the suppliers benefiting from it.

Less than three months later, the financing arrangements have expanded considerably. Nvidia is supporting AI infrastructure development through equity investments, credit commitments and partnerships with major financial institutions. Meanwhile, Broadcom, Oracle and SpaceX are pursuing financing arrangements involving tens of billions of dollars to acquire or deploy AI computing hardware. The structures differ, but they demonstrate how access to capital is becoming as important as access to processors in determining which companies can participate in the AI infrastructure expansion.

The underlying economic question is becoming more significant as infrastructure commitments increase. Semiconductor suppliers recognize revenue when processors and networking systems are delivered, while the customers purchasing those systems may require years to generate sufficient operating cash flow to justify the investment. Financing can bridge that gap, but it does not eliminate the requirement that the completed infrastructure eventually produce an adequate return.

Nvidia Established the Model

Nvidia’s financing strategy initially developed around direct investments in AI customers and infrastructure providers. Its relationship with CoreWeave (CRWV) is particularly instructive. Nvidia invested $2 billion in CoreWeave common stock, while CoreWeave built its computing infrastructure primarily around Nvidia processors. Under a separate $6.3 billion agreement, Nvidia committed to purchasing CoreWeave cloud capacity that remained unsold to other customers through April 2032.

The arrangement connected three financial relationships. Nvidia supplied the processors generating its semiconductor revenue, invested in the cloud provider purchasing those processors, and supported that provider’s future revenue through a capacity-purchase commitment. Each transaction could be commercially justified independently, but together they demonstrated how supplier capital and customer demand could reinforce one another.

Nvidia subsequently extended this approach through its relationship with OpenAI. The companies announced a framework under which Nvidia intended to invest as much as $100 billion as OpenAI deployed at least 10 gigawatts of Nvidia computing systems. The proposed investments were directly connected to the deployment of Nvidia hardware, making the financial relationship more explicit than a conventional supplier-customer agreement.

The financing model has since expanded beyond equity investments. Nvidia has disclosed substantial commitments associated with AI infrastructure, including support for cloud providers and potential credit exposure related to major data-center projects. Its involvement with institutional investors also creates opportunities to mobilize capital without financing every facility directly from Nvidia’s own balance sheet.

This is an important strategic advantage. Nvidia is no longer competing solely on GPU performance, networking technology and software compatibility. Its financial relationships can also help customers secure the capital required to deploy Nvidia-based infrastructure. Competitors attempting to win major AI contracts must increasingly address both the technical requirements of their processors and the financial requirements of their customers.

According to Chart 1, financial support from semiconductor suppliers can help customers purchase computing systems, generating revenue for the same suppliers providing that support. The distinction between supplier-financed demand and independently financed demand becomes particularly important when investors attempt to determine whether reported semiconductor revenue reflects sustainable end-market economics.

text:
The African banking group strengthens its international footprint with a French presence aimed at deepening trade, investment and financial ties between Africa, Europe and global markets.

By Ajong Mbapndah L

Vista Bank is extending its international ambitions with the introduction of Vista Bank France, marking another important chapter in the African banking group’s expansion and its efforts to strengthen financial connections between the continent and major international markets.

Announced under the banner “From Africa, to Paris and the World Beyond,” the development brings Vista’s growing banking network closer to one of Europe’s leading financial centres. The French operation is expected to provide a platform for supporting cross-border business, facilitating international transactions and expanding financial services for companies and institutions operating between Africa and Europe.

The expansion comes against the backdrop of growing commercial ties between African economies and international markets, with businesses increasingly seeking reliable banking partners capable of supporting trade, investment and cross-border transactions. France, with its longstanding economic relationships across Francophone Africa and its position as a major European financial hub, offers Vista an important base from which to pursue these opportunities.

For African businesses seeking access to European markets, the presence of an African-rooted banking group in Paris could help bridge some of the financial and institutional gaps that complicate international commerce. Trade finance, correspondent banking, foreign exchange services and corporate financing are among the areas where Vista hopes to make its presence felt.

The foundation for the French expansion was laid in January 2025, when Vista Group announced that it had secured approval from France’s Prudential Supervision and Resolution Authority (ACPR) to establish Vista Bank France. The approval represented an important milestone for the group, which has pursued an ambitious expansion strategy through acquisitions and investments in banking operations across Africa.

Simon Tiemtore, Chairman of Vista Group Holding, has been central to that expansion, overseeing the group’s efforts to build a banking network capable of serving African businesses while strengthening their access to international financial markets. Under his leadership, Vista has expanded its interests across West and Central Africa, targeting markets where banking penetration, access to credit and financing for small and medium-sized enterprises remain important development priorities.

The French operation adds an international dimension to that strategy. Vista Bank France is expected to offer services including correspondent banking, corporate banking, international trade finance, factoring, foreign exchange, treasury management and financial advisory services, providing businesses with additional options for managing their international operations.

Vista’s expansion into France is also noteworthy at a time when the relationship between African and European banking institutions is undergoing significant changes. Several major European banking groups have reduced or restructured their African operations in recent years, creating opportunities for African investors and financial institutions to acquire established banking businesses and strengthen their positions in regional markets.

Vista has been among the groups taking advantage of these changes. Its acquisition of Banco Société Générale Moçambique in 2024 and the completion of its majority acquisition of Société Générale Burkina Faso in 2025 form part of a wider strategy to expand its banking network and deepen its presence in African economies.

These acquisitions have given Vista access to established banking infrastructure, customer relationships and markets where demand for financial services continues to grow. They have also strengthened the group’s capacity to serve corporate clients, entrepreneurs and businesses involved in domestic and international trade.

The establishment of Vista Bank France brings a different set of opportunities. Rather than concentrating exclusively on expanding its African banking network, the group is now seeking to position itself closer to international financial institutions, European investors and businesses with commercial interests on the continent.

For African exporters, importers and companies pursuing international partnerships, access to banking services that understand both African operating environments and European financial requirements can be particularly valuable. Difficulties securing trade finance, managing foreign exchange transactions and accessing international payment systems remain familiar challenges for businesses across the continent.

Vista’s ability to address some of these constraints will be an important test of its international expansion. The group’s established relationships in African markets could provide an advantage in serving clients whose operations span several countries, although its success will depend on the competitiveness of its services and the strength of its international banking relationships.

The development also reflects the growing confidence of African financial institutions in pursuing opportunities beyond the continent. While European banks have maintained a presence in African markets for decades, African banking groups are increasingly building the capital, networks and institutional capacity to compete internationally.

Vista Bank France enters this landscape with an identity firmly rooted in Africa and a business proposition centred on international growth. Its promotional campaign highlights service, strength and vision, qualities the group will be expected to demonstrate as it builds its presence in the French market.

For Simon Tiemtore and Vista Group, the French expansion represents more than the addition of another market to the group’s portfolio. It provides an opportunity to connect its African banking operations more directly with European financial markets and develop relationships that could support businesses on both continents.

Much will depend on how Vista Bank France develops its client base, builds partnerships and delivers on its proposed services. With its African network continuing to expand, the Paris operation could become an important part of the group’s efforts to serve companies whose financing needs increasingly extend beyond national and continental borders.

text:
Kroger says it will cut 3,000 corporate jobs over the next three years as CEO Greg Foran accelerates the grocery chain's use of artificial intelligence.

The move comes as the company faces mounting pressure from Walmart, discount grocers Aldi and Lidl, and Amazon.

Here's what to know

According to ClickOrlando.com, Kroger has told employees it will cut 3,000 corporate positions over three years while increasing its use of AI to make operations more efficient.

Based in Cincinnati, the company is the country's largest standalone supermarket chain, with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith's, and Fred Meyer.

Foran described the shift in a memo to employees, writing: "Technology is reshaping what's possible. The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work, and look closely at where work is best fit to be done."

Wall Street's early reaction appeared cautious, with Kroger stock down 1.6% to $61.66 in early trading on Oct. 13. Kroger had already outlined an AI strategy tied to improving the customer experience, making work easier for associates, and producing better business outcomes.

More background

Foran became Kroger's CEO in February, stepping in 11 months after the previous chief executive's abrupt departure. He ran Walmart's U.S. division from 2014 to 2019 and built a reputation as a tech-minded, detail-focused operator.

While at Walmart, Foran pushed for cleaner stores, better product availability, and a stronger fresh produce department. He also expanded online ordering and pickup, accelerating Walmart's digital growth.

After Kroger failed to complete its proposed Albertsons merger, the company continued to face competitive pressure from Aldi, Lidl, and Amazon. The deal was proposed in 2022, but in 2024, the Federal Trade Commission and the states of Washington and Colorado sued to stop it. They argued that it would reduce competition, raise prices, and suppress workers' wages.

Courts ultimately ruled that the merger would not move forward. After the deal collapsed, Albertsons sued Kroger for a $600 million breakup fee plus billions in legal costs and lost shareholder value, and Kroger called the claims "baseless," according to ClickOrlando.com.

What's being done?

Kroger says the AI push is intended to benefit both customers and store associates, but it is also central to a companywide efficiency effort. In Foran's memo, the job cuts were presented as part of adopting new capabilities and reconsidering how work is assigned.

The strategy pairs efforts to sharpen operations in a fiercely competitive market with the costs and consequences of deploying more advanced tech at scale. With the Albertsons merger blocked, Kroger appears to be betting more heavily on internal transformation instead.

text:
In a bold move to solidify its position at the pinnacle of international premium travel, Delta Air Lines has unveiled a comprehensive overhaul of its signature Delta One cabin experience.

The multi-million-dollar elevation spans re-engineered suite architecture, elevated ground service, hyper-personalised inflight hospitality, and chef-curated culinary offerings, setting a high benchmark for transatlantic and transpacific competition.

The announcement comes as global carriers aggressively compete for premium passenger yields on key international corridors, where high-yielding business class revenues continue to outperform pre-pandemic baselines.

At the heart of the upgrade is a suite enclosure with full-height sliding privacy doors, improved ergonomics, and customizable ambient mood lighting.

Each Delta One suite features ultra-premium memory-foam seating that transforms seamlessly into a 180-degree flat bed, with increased seat width and expanded side storage for personal technology and essentials.

The cabin architecture integrates high-definition 21-inch 4K screen displays among the largest in business class globally, paired with high-speed Bluetooth audio connectivity and high-output USB-C fast charging at every seat.

To boost passenger wellness on ultra-long-haul routes, Delta has partnered with leading luxury sleepwear and bedding brands to introduce breathable, eco-friendly linens made from 100% recycled materials, alongside refreshed luxury amenity kits.

Delta’s investment extends well beyond the aircraft cabin, focusing heavily on a seamless end-to-end journey for Delta One travellers.

Building on the flagship Delta One Lounge opening at New York-JFK, the carrier is accelerating dedicated private lounge developments at major hubs including Los Angeles (LAX), Boston (BOS), and Seattle (SEA).

These exclusive spaces feature private check-in corridors, dedicated TSA security checkpoints, à la carte fine dining, and spa facilities.

The inflight dining service has been overhauled in collaboration with Michelin-recognised chefs, featuring regionally inspired multi-course menus tailored to specific flight origin points, complemented by a curated wine list from master sommeliers.

A revamped, personalised cabin service protocol lets passengers control the pace of service, with options for expedited dining or scheduled sleep intervals.

As air transport economics increasingly weigh premium yield expansion, Delta’s overhaul directly challenges North American and European rivals on core intercontinental routes.

By standardising a high-density, high-privacy suite concept across its wide-body fleet while expanding dedicated ground infrastructure, Delta aims to capture an even larger share of premium corporate and high-end leisure travel markets.

The upgraded Delta One suites are scheduled to debut on international long-haul routes starting in early 2027.

title: OpenAI Humanoid Robot: Altman Eyes 2027 Demo
description:
OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, and CEO Sam Altman says the machine’s body is the easier half of the job.
Speaking on the Sources podcast in early September, Altman answered a question about whether OpenAI’s hardware push meant a humanoid or a data-centre machine with “Both”, as Forbes reported.
According to dev.ua’s relay of the interview, Altman told Fortune that OpenAI should have a demo in 2027.
When will OpenAI’s humanoid robot launch?
Will the OpenAI robot be for homes?
text:
OpenAI is building a humanoid robot, and CEO Sam Altman says the machine’s body is the easier half of the job. Speaking on the Sources podcast in early September, Altman answered a question about whether OpenAI’s hardware push meant a humanoid or a data-centre machine with “Both”, as Forbes reported. “We will definitely do a humanoid,” he said. “We will do other form factors as well.” Engadget’s latest write-up pulls the remarks together with a rough timeline.

That timeline is the newest detail. According to dev.ua’s relay of the interview, Altman told Fortune that OpenAI should have a demo in 2027. Engadget quotes him as saying robots won’t be walking the streets for a few years after that. OpenAI hasn’t said what the demo will show or what the robot will look like, so for now this is a CEO’s target rather than a product plan.

Why a humanoid, and why the brain comes first

Altman’s case for the human shape is practical. On the podcast, he argued that “the world is very much designed for people,” and that doors, keyboards and tools assume a human body. A robot that works in those spaces without modification should probably match that form. Where the body ends up looking is, in his words, “less important than really figuring out … the brain that makes the robot work.”

That’s the harder problem. A useful humanoid has to read its cameras and sensors, interpret instructions, plan the task, coordinate its limbs, and recover when something goes wrong. Picking up a mug means finding the handle, judging the grip, and applying the right force, or you spill. OpenAI has been here before: its Dactyl project trained a robotic hand to handle real objects entirely in simulation, and the company later applied the approach to a Rubik’s Cube. Models can learn the right move in software, but physics still decides whether it works.

The body isn’t an afterthought

Altman’s emphasis on software doesn’t mean OpenAI is ignoring hardware. Engadget’s reading of the company’s robotics listings shows work on custom electromechanical actuators, including motors, transmissions, sensing and thermal systems, plus roles in manufacturing and the supply chain needed to produce hardware at scale. Other roles cover motion control, state estimation, actuator control and the machine-learning infrastructure for training physical AI. Engadget counts 27 robotics openings on OpenAI’s careers page.

The company isn’t alone. Tesla has worked on Optimus for years, and XPENG recently had its IRON humanoid walk off the production line on its own after assembly. Both show how much effort it takes to get a complex set of motors and joints to behave, even with capable software.

The first target isn’t the living room. According to Engadget, one of OpenAI’s robotics postings names general-purpose robots that help skilled workers build infrastructure as the short-term goal, with a personal robot that handles a wider range of tasks as the long-term one. Because a home robot would carry cameras and microphones into private spaces, it will raise privacy questions, though OpenAI hasn’t announced a price, subscription model, release date, or robot-specific privacy framework.

When will OpenAI’s humanoid robot launch?

There’s no release date. Altman told Fortune he expects a demo in 2027 and doesn’t expect robots on the streets for a few years after that, so a consumer product is further out still.

Will the OpenAI robot be for homes?

Not first. OpenAI’s job postings describe infrastructure-building robots that assist skilled workers as the near-term goal, and a personal robot as the longer-term one.
