Domino’s Pizza Q3 U.S. same-store sales growth slowed to 0.3%.

CEO Joe Jordan said budget-conscious customers are ordering fewer items.

The company expects consumer pressures to persist through 2026.

Domino’s Pizza Inc. (DPZ) stock is heading for a weekly loss after its third-quarter (Q3) results beat Wall Street estimates but showed customers cutting back on orders to protect their budgets. New CEO Joe Jordan warned that consumer pressure would persist through year-end and guided for U.S. same-store sales growth at the low end of its forecast range.

Domino’s Pizza stock edged up 0.6% overnight ahead of Wednesday, after dropping more than 4% in the regular session.

Domino’s Q3 Earnings Beat Mask Weakening Same-Store Sales Growth

Tuesday’s stock decline ends a two-week winning streak and highlights the central tension in the Domino’s story. Customers are still ordering, but they are buying less each time. On the surface, the quarter was solid. Domino’s reported net income of $152.2 million, or $4.60 per share, up from $139.3 million, or $4.08, a year earlier. Revenue rose to $1.19 billion from $1.15 billion. Both topped the analysts’ consensus estimates of $1.17 billion and $4.38, respectively, according to Fiscal.ai data.

Advertisement|Remove ads.

The growth quality is the concern. U.S. same-store sales rose just 0.3%, a sharp deceleration from 5.2% in the year-ago quarter. International same-store sales rose 0.2%. Global retail sales growth slowed to 3.2% from 6.3%, reaching $4.84 billion. Store count grew 4.4%, so expansion, not existing locations, is doing the heavy lifting. With the stock down about 29% year-to-date, investors are weighing whether the pizza giant’s value strategy can protect profits when consumers are stretched.

The quarterly trend shows the slide. Domino’s U.S. same-store sales growth has swung sharply over the past three years while its operating margin has stayed steady. Comparable sales peaked at 5.6% in Q1 2024 and again at 5.2% in Q3 2025, but have since faded to 3.7% in Q4 2025, 0.9% in Q1 2026, 0.1% in Q2 and just 0.3% in Q3 2026, which is roughly flat.

Operating margin has stayed between roughly 17% and 20%, rising from 17.3% in Q1 2023 to a high of 20.4% in Q3 2026. This suggests Domino’s franchise-based business is helping protect profits. However, same-store sales growth only edged up to 0.3% in Q3.

Advertisement|Remove ads.

Domino’s Sees Smaller Orders As Consumer Pressures Persist

It was Jordan’s first earnings call as CEO. He succeeded Russell Weiner this month after serving as chief operating officer, and his message was blunt about where the strain shows up.

“So the brand is still relevant, even when the pressure is on their pocketbooks,” Jordan said. “But in Q3, we believe that manifested mostly in items per order. So we had pressure on items per order, so customers were still coming to us, but managing their ticket by managing items per order.”

Advertisement|Remove ads.

In other words, traffic is not the problem. Basket size is. Diners are skipping the extra side, dessert, or second pizza, even as they keep choosing Domino’s for dinner. Jordan offered little near-term relief. “Looking ahead to the remainder of 2026, we expect the macro environment to remain an overhang on the consumer through the balance of the year.”

CFO Sandeep Reddy put numbers on that caution. Domino’s still expects U.S. comparable sales to rise at a low-single-digit rate, but Reddy said that after three quarters, the company believes it will land “towards the low end of that range.” That assumes the “challenging macroeconomic and competitive environment” seen so far persists.

International is weaker. Domino’s now expects international same-store sales growth to be roughly flat for the year, citing continued pressure at DPE, its Domino’s Pizza Enterprises franchise partner.

Advertisement|Remove ads.

Wall Street Reacts To Domino’s Q3 Performance

TD Cowen kept its ‘Hold’ rating and $320 price target. The analyst noted that management alluded to continued ticket pressure in Q4 amid “no quick fix” in a challenged pizza category. The firm cut its Q4 U.S. comp estimate to 1% from 1.5%. It also does not expect “sweeping changes” when Jordan lays out his strategic plan with Q4 results.

Morningstar analyst Ari Felhandler remained positive about Domino’s despite trimming his forecasts. He believes discounts are attracting cost-conscious customers, while rising orders show that the company’s affordable prices and new menu items are appealing amid economic uncertainty and heavy competition.

Domino’s marketing muscle and franchisee model may give it more room to price aggressively than rivals such as Papa John’s International (PZZA) and Yum! Brands (YUM), parent of Pizza Hut. Morningstar expects the chain to use targeted promotions to increase items per order, which could boost restaurant-level profit.

Advertisement|Remove ads.

Still, the weaker outlook is changing the growth math. Morningstar cut its 2026 U.S. net store opening forecast to 125 to 150, in line with management’s revised target and down from its prior estimate of 167. It sees roughly 75 openings in 2027 as competition and soft domestic demand weigh on expansion.

Several of the country's largest health insurers have joined a new group that aims to make the doctor information in their online directories more reliable.
DataSpring, the insurer-owned data company formerly known as CAQH, announced the Provider Data Collective and its first standard on October 13.
DataSpring describes its provider data portal as the central repository for 80% of licensed U.S. clinicians.

text:
Several of the country's largest health insurers have joined a new group that aims to make the doctor information in their online directories more reliable. DataSpring, the insurer-owned data company formerly known as CAQH, announced the Provider Data Collective and its first standard on October 13.

Founding members are Aetna, Centene, The Cigna Group, Elevance Health, Horizon Healthcare Services, Humana, and UnitedHealth Group, along with the American Medical Association (AMA), the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), and DataSpring itself. The group's first product is a common way to measure the quality of directory data for individual clinicians, including office locations, whether a doctor is accepting new patients, which health plans they take, and their licenses and credentials. DataSpring said the framework builds on the quality foundation the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) uses for provider directories and was developed in three months. The group said its next focus will be how a doctor's "accepting new patients" status is determined, updated, and displayed.

The timing matters for millions of households. Medicare open enrollment runs from October 15 to December 7, 2026, for coverage that starts January 1, 2027, and many older adults compare plans largely by which doctors they can see. A new measurement standard will not clean up listings this season, so patients still need to check before they choose.

An Insurer-Owned Data Hub Sets the Ground Rules

DataSpring sits in the middle of how many directories are built. The company maintains more than 4.8 million provider records and links eligibility information for more than three-quarters of covered patients in the United States, according to Becker's coverage of the CAQH rebrand. Clinicians enter their practice details once, and participating insurers draw from that record. DataSpring describes its provider data portal as the central repository for 80% of licensed U.S. clinicians.

That structure also explains how errors spread. When a doctor moves, changes hours, or stops accepting a plan, the update has to reach many insurers that copy and display the information in different ways. One stale entry can show up in several directories at once.

Chief Executive Sarah Ahmad told Becker's in June that the company planned to bring organizations together and "set a data quality standard for the country that everybody can use." DataSpring has also described a collaborative initiative with 12 health plans, including several Blue Cross Blue Shield companies and Kaiser Permanente, to improve provider data and reduce paperwork for doctors.

The arrangement raises a fair accountability question. The standard comes from a company that insurers own, and those same insurers publish the directories being measured. The AMA and NCQA add outside voices, but the announcement did not say whether adoption will be required, how the standard will be enforced, or whether accuracy results will be made public. DataSpring said only that the standard could inform regulators as they update provider data rules.

Directory Errors Have Been Documented for Years

The problem is well established. In a CMS review of Medicare Advantage directories conducted from November 2017 to July 2018, 48.74% of the 10,504 provider locations checked had at least one inaccuracy, such as a provider not working at the listed location, a wrong phone number, or a doctor listed as accepting new patients who was not. The American Psychiatric Association cited that figure in testimony for a May 2023 Senate Finance Committee hearing on ghost networks in mental health care.

Federal law already sets basic rules for most private health plans. Under the No Surprises Act, in effect since January 1, 2022, plans must verify directory information at least every 90 days, update it within two business days of a change, and answer questions about a provider's network status within one business day. If you rely on a wrong directory listing or plan response and get care from an out-of-network provider, the plan generally can charge you only in-network cost sharing.

Medicare Advantage plans face new requirements soon. The REAL Health Providers Act, written by Rep. Jimmy Panetta of California, became law as part of a federal spending package in February 2026. Starting in 2028, it requires Medicare Advantage plans to verify directory data regularly, remove providers who have left the network within five business days, and run annual accuracy audits. Plans must post accuracy scores starting in 2029. Panetta said, "I wrote a straightforward bill that directly fixes the problem by reducing and tightening up these Ghost Networks."

Advocates have pushed for broader fixes. Alan Nessman, senior special counsel at the American Psychological Association, told Managed Healthcare Executive in 2023 that the group was advocating for "simple standardized reporting for all insurers and, ideally, a national provider directory."

The burden falls hardest on people who need care quickly or need a specialist in short supply. That includes patients seeking therapists or psychiatrists, older adults new to Medicare Advantage, families in rural areas with few nearby options, and anyone who cannot spend hours on the phone.

A Five-Minute Check Before You Book or Switch Plans

Call the doctor's office directly instead of relying only on the website. Give the exact name of your plan, not just the insurer, because a practice may accept one product and not another. Ask whether the doctor is in-network for that specific plan and whether they are accepting new patients under it.

Keep a record. Take a dated screenshot of the directory listing and note the name of the person you spoke with on each call. If you later receive an out-of-network bill after relying on the directory, that record can support an appeal.

If you cannot find an in-network provider, call your plan's member services and ask for help locating one. You can file a complaint with your state insurance department, or with Medicare for Medicare plans. The federal No Surprises Help Desk, at 1-800-985-3059, answers questions about medical bills and whether the No Surprises Act applies.

People comparing Medicare plans before December 7 should confirm their key doctors and hospitals with each office, not only through the online plan finder. That includes doctors you have seen for years.

Insurers have not said when patients will notice cleaner listings or whether results under the new standard will be shared with the public or regulators.

Key Questions Answered

What did insurers announce? DataSpring, an insurer-owned data company, launched the Provider Data Collective with Aetna, Centene, Cigna, Elevance Health, Horizon, Humana, UnitedHealth Group, the AMA, and NCQA. Its first product is a shared standard for measuring the quality of clinician directory data.

Will my insurer's directory be fixed right away? No. The standard sets a common way to measure data quality, but insurers have not said when patients will see more accurate listings.

What is a ghost network? It is a plan's provider list that includes doctors who cannot be reached, are out of network, or are not taking new patients, even though they appear available.

What protections do I have now? The No Surprises Act requires most plans to verify directory data at least every 90 days and generally limits you to in-network costs if you relied on a wrong listing. Stricter Medicare Advantage directory rules begin in 2028.

How can I confirm a doctor takes my plan? Call the office, name your exact plan, ask about new patients, and save a dated screenshot of the directory listing.

Where can I complain about directory errors? Contact your plan first, then your state insurance department, Medicare for Medicare plans, or the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059.

text:
Agilent Technologies has agreed to acquire Proscia, a provider of digital pathology software for clinical and life sciences customers, in an all-cash transaction valued at $240 million at closing plus up to $30 million tied to future performance milestones.

The acquisition will expand Agilent’s pathology business by combining its instruments and reagents with Proscia’s digital pathology software platform. Agilent said the combination will strengthen its position in the approximately $5 billion pathology market while creating a broader platform for AI-enabled scientific intelligence and tissue-based precision medicine.

Proscia’s software serves as an operating layer for digital pathology, connecting slide scanners, laboratory information systems, image-analysis applications, AI tools, people, and data within a unified environment. The platform is designed to help clinical and life sciences organizations manage pathology images, data, and workflows.

Proscia currently serves more than 4,000 laboratories, hospitals, and clinics, along with 16 of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies. The business generated more than $18 million in revenue during the trailing 12 months and operates with a recurring-revenue software model.

The companies already have an established relationship. Agilent and Proscia entered into a multi-year distribution agreement in September 2022 to offer a comprehensive digital diagnostic pathology system. The acquisition builds on that partnership and follows Agilent’s recent transaction involving Biocare Medical.

Agilent plans to integrate Proscia’s vendor-agnostic digital pathology platform with its existing pathology instrumentation and reagent portfolio. Proscia’s platform has received FDA 510(k) clearance for primary diagnosis, positioning the combined business to support laboratories as pathology workflows increasingly move toward digital and AI-enabled systems.

The transaction is also expected to strengthen Agilent’s companion diagnostics and biopharmaceutical drug discovery offerings. Proscia’s growing repository of real-world pathology data could support additional AI-enabled applications across Agilent’s companion diagnostics business and help pharmaceutical companies and researchers extract insights from tissue data.

Agilent said Proscia will also add a high-growth, high-margin recurring software business to its pathology portfolio. The company sees opportunities to connect pathology data generation with AI-based interpretation across workflows ranging from biomarker research and clinical development to routine diagnostics.

The acquisition is expected to close early in Agilent’s fiscal year 2027, subject to customary closing conditions. Following completion, Proscia will become part of the Agilent Life Sciences and Diagnostics Markets Group.

Agilent generated $6.95 billion in revenue during fiscal 2025 and employs approximately 18,000 people worldwide. DLA Piper is serving as legal adviser to Agilent, while Cooley is serving as legal adviser to Proscia. Joele Frank is advising Agilent on strategic communications.

KEY QUOTES:

“Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market. The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use. With Proscia’s leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data. We look forward to welcoming the Proscia team to Agilent and working together to accelerate adoption of AI-enabled pathology workflows to advance drug discovery and companion-diagnostics solutions and create long-term value for customers and shareholders.”

Padraig McDonnell, President And CEO Of Agilent

“This agreement with Agilent marks an exciting milestone for Proscia and reflects the strength of the platform our team has built. Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions. Together, we can accelerate innovation while continuing to provide customers with the flexibility they need across clinical and life-sciences workflows. I am grateful to the entire Proscia team, whose dedication made this milestone possible, and look forward to building on our work as part of Agilent.”

title: Delta Air Lines' Next Widebody Will Carry 101 Premium Seats & Barely Any Economy
description:

The planned configuration includes 53 Delta One suites and 48 Premium Select seats, giving it 101 seats across those two premium cabins.
Delta has also highlighted Delta Comfort as part of the A350-1000's premium mix, bringing the proportion of seats categorized as premium to around 50%.

Premium Economy gives Delta another option for customers who want more space and comfort without paying for business class.
text:
Delta Air Lines is preparing to introduce a widebody aircraft that reflects its changing business model. The Airbus A350-1000 will feature 101 premium seats, including 53 business-class suites and 48 premium economy seats, giving front-of-cabin passengers far more prominence than on a conventional long-haul configuration. The surprising part is what the decision says about the airline's priorities.

For years, filling economy cabins was central to long-haul economics, with premium seats providing a valuable supplement to the revenue generated at the back of the aircraft. Delta's latest financial results suggest that balance is shifting. With premium ticket revenue overtaking Main Cabin revenue for the first time in the second quarter of 2026, CEO Ed Bastian and his team have a powerful financial incentive to rethink the traditional widebody cabin. The question is how the A350-1000 will turn that strategy into a competitive advantage, and what it means for the passengers who will occupy the remaining economy seats.

Why Delta's A350-1000 Is Different From A Conventional Long-Haul Aircraft

The answer begins with Delta's decision to make the Airbus A350-1000 its most premium-focused aircraft. The airline unveiled its next-generation Delta One suite in April 2026, confirming that the new widebody would deliver a substantially upgraded business-class experience and a redesigned premium economy cabin. The aircraft is expected to begin arriving in 2027, making it an important part of Delta's next phase of international fleet development. Delta's official announcement best indicates how the airline intends to differentiate the aircraft.

The planned configuration includes 53 Delta One suites and 48 Premium Select seats, giving it 101 seats across those two premium cabins. That is a significant commitment to higher-priced travel, particularly when compared with Delta's existing A350-900s, which have 32 Delta One seats and 48 Premium Select seats in their published configuration. As a result, the A350-1000 will have 21 more business-class suites than the A350-900, an increase of about 66%. You can compare the existing aircraft layout with Delta's A350-900 seat specifications.

However, an important distinction exists between the 101 seats in the two premium cabins and the airline's broader definition of premium seating. Delta has also highlighted Delta Comfort as part of the A350-1000's premium mix, bringing the proportion of seats categorized as premium to around 50%. The aircraft will still carry a substantial economy cabin, so the change does not eliminate affordable seating. Instead, Delta is allocating more of its aircraft to products that can command higher fares and encourage customers to spend more on each journey. Why is the airline so confident that demand will support this approach?

Premium Ticket Revenue Has Finally Overtaken Main Cabin

Delta's second-quarter 2026 results provide the clearest financial explanation. In the three months ended June 30, premium ticket revenue reached $6.92 billion, up from $6.85 billion in Main Cabin tickets. The difference was relatively narrow (about $69 million), but the milestone was significant because premium ticket sales had overtaken Main Cabin ticket sales for the first time. According to Delta's June-quarter financial results, premium ticket revenue increased 17% year over year, compared with 8% growth in Main Cabin ticket revenue.

However, Delta's broader financial picture extends beyond ticket sales. The airline reported that diversified revenue streams accounted for 61% of total revenue in the quarter, up two percentage points from a year earlier. That category includes premium products and other sources such as loyalty, cargo, and maintenance, repair, and overhaul services. It would be inaccurate to interpret the 61% figure as premium ticket revenue alone, but it demonstrates how much Delta's financial performance now depends on businesses beyond conventional economy fares.

The company is also benefiting from strong corporate demand. Delta reported that premium corporate sales rose more than 25%, with investments in Delta Comfort and Premium Select driving the growth. For the A350-1000, this creates a compelling commercial opportunity: the aircraft can serve business travelers willing to pay for privacy and a lie-flat bed while also offering a more comfortable alternative to standard economy for travelers who do not require a business-class suite. But the revenue crossover raises another question: is Delta simply responding to demand, or is it actively reshaping the market it wants to serve?

Delta Is Choosing Higher Yields Over Main Cabin Seat Growth

Delta's strategy focuses more on each seat's value than on how many seats it can sell. CEO Ed Bastian and Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito have said the airline intends to prioritize premium demand rather than continue expanding Main Cabin capacity as its main growth strategy. Their comments, reported in the Q2 2026 earnings call transcript, reflect a wider effort to move away from competing primarily on the lowest available fare.

That does not mean Delta is abandoning economy passengers. Its Main Cabin revenue still increased year over year, and the airline continues to sell hundreds of economy seats on its widebody aircraft. Instead, the company is placing greater emphasis on its seat mix, the fares those seats can generate, and the additional spending they can encourage. A premium seat can generate substantially more revenue than a standard economy seat, though the actual difference depends on the route, demand, season, and the cost of providing the service.

The economics matter most when operating expenses rise. Delta reported an adjusted fuel price of $3.93 per gallon in the June quarter, up 75% from a year earlier, while adjusted fuel expense rose 77%. Those figures, included in the official earnings release, show why airlines have an incentive to extract more revenue from their available capacity. Higher fares cannot automatically offset every increase in fuel, labor, or aircraft costs, but stronger premium yields can help protect margins.

For the A350-1000, the decision goes far beyond the cabin design. Delta is investing in an aircraft that can concentrate more of its business-class capacity into private suites while expanding its premium economy offering. That configuration could be particularly attractive on long-haul routes where corporate travelers, affluent leisure passengers and customers using loyalty benefits create demand for higher-priced products. The next question is whether Delta's investment stops with the new aircraft or extends to the rest of its widebody fleet.

The A350-1000 Is Only One Part Of Delta's Premium Overhaul

Delta is also investing in new and existing aircraft, so the A350-1000 will not be the only widebody offering an upgraded business-class experience. Delta has also ordered 30 Boeing 787-10s with a premium heavy cabin. Regarding existing planes, the airline has announced a program costing more than $1 billion to refresh its cabins, including extensive work on 42 Airbus A330-200 and A330-300 aircraft. The aircraft will receive Delta One suites with privacy doors and cabin-wide updates. Every seat on the refreshed A330S and the new A350-1000 will get larger seatback screens, Bluetooth connectivity, USB-C charging, and universal power outlets. Details of the investment and cabin changes are available in Delta's announcement of its next-generation suites. You can also check our detailed seat maps here.

Essentially, Delta is pursuing a fleet-wide product strategy. A passenger flying on a refreshed A330 should get a more consistent premium experience, even if the aircraft doesn't offer the same configuration as the A350-1000. Delta expects more than 800 aircraft to receive its modern interiors over the next five years, giving the program a much wider reach than the new A350 variant alone.

The business-class seat is central to that investment. Delta developed its next-generation Delta One suite through a two-year design process informed by a decade of customer and employee feedback. Privacy doors are intended to give passengers a more enclosed personal space, while improved screens and charging options address expectations that have become increasingly important on long-haul journeys. Delta has also announced plans to expand suite availability across its fleet, with The Points Guy's coverage of the cabin program adding context.

The strategy also has a competitive dimension. Delta is trying to distinguish its long-haul product through the overall experience, not by the number of seats in each cabin. A modern business-class suite may help attract customers who compare airlines on privacy, comfort, and onboard technology rather than fare alone. Yet premium seating is only valuable if travelers consistently pay for it, which makes Delta's loyalty program and its relationship with American Express very important.

Why American Express And SkyMiles Are Central To The Aircraft's Economics

Delta's premium strategy extends beyond the aircraft itself. Its relationship with American Express generates substantial revenue through the co-branded card partnership, helping the airline earn money from customers even when they are not purchasing a flight. In 2025, American Express remuneration reached $8.2 billion, up 11% from the previous year, according to Delta's full-year financial results. Delta's longer-term target is to reach approximately $9 billion in remuneration in 2026.

That income stream strengthens the airline's ability to invest in premium cabins, airport lounges, and onboard amenities. It also gives Delta more opportunities to build customer relationships through SkyMiles, credit-card benefits, and travel-related spending. The connection isn't that every cardholder will purchase a Delta One suite, but that the airline has built a system where loyalty engagement and premium travel reinforce one another.

The A350-1000 fits into this system by offering a more differentiated product for customers who highly value comfort. Premium passengers may pay more for a lie-flat bed, a private suite, and lounge access, while frequent travelers can also use miles or other benefits to improve their experience. Premium Economy gives Delta another option for customers who want more space and comfort without paying for business class. According to Delta's Premium Select product information, the cabin offers more personal space, wider seats, and greater recline than standard economy.

Nevertheless, loyalty revenue and premium ticket revenue are not the same. The former includes payments tied to Delta's partnership and broader loyalty network, while the latter reflects revenue from premium airline tickets. Together, they help explain why the airline invests heavily in cabin upgrades, but they don't guarantee every premium seat will command a high fare on every flight. The remaining challenge is making the aircraft's economics work when demand weakens, or passengers become more price-sensitive.

Delta's A350-1000 Will Test How Far Premium-First Flying Can Go

The A350-1000 represents a long-term bet that Delta can earn more by improving the value of its passenger offering than by continually expanding the number of economy seats available. That approach matters most on long-haul routes, where business-class suites and premium economy can support a differentiated product while the aircraft continues to carry passengers on more affordable fares. The new configuration does not eliminate economy, but it places premium cabins at the center of the aircraft's commercial proposition.

There is also a competitive context. Delta has committed to ordering 20 A350-1000s, a fleet decision that signals the aircraft's substantial role in its future long-haul network. As discussed in our analysis of Delta's A350-1000 order, the order points toward a different approach to international growth, with the aircraft's size and premium cabin configuration central to the airline's plans.

Still, the strategy carries risks. Premium demand can shift with corporate travel budgets, economic conditions, and competition from other airlines. A more expensive cabin also needs sufficient demand across seasons, and no amount of cabin refinement can guarantee premium fares will remain high. Delta's second-quarter results underscore the pressure: despite strong revenue growth, adjusted fuel expense rose sharply, showing how external costs can erode the benefits of stronger ticket sales.

The aircraft's arrival in 2027 will mark a fleet milestone and provide a practical test of whether Delta can translate its premium-revenue lead into sustained returns on a new generation of long-haul aircraft. The airline has already demonstrated that premium tickets can generate more revenue than Main Cabin tickets in a quarter. The next challenge is to prove that a premium-focused cabin can deliver the same commercial advantage over the aircraft's life.

text:
Milan-based bank UniCredit has received the go-ahead from the supervisory authority of the European Central Bank (ECB) to acquire more Commerzbank shares and ultimately to take control of the German bank, the Italian lender said on Thursday.

This means that UniCredit can convert the Commerzbank shares it already acquired earlier in the year via an exchange offer into its own shares.

UniCredit said the ECB had approved its bid to acquire control of Commerzbank. It said it had received approval to cross the 30% threshold of Commerzbank's share capital and to keep increasing its stake without an upper limit.

"The decision represents an important milestone in UniCredit's acquisition of Commerzbank, underscoring the ECB's positive assessment of the transaction and the confidence in UniCredit's solid fundamentals and strong standing within the European banking sector," the bank added.

Remaining regulatory procedures and conditions for completing the offer for Commerzbank are expected to be concluded by year-end, according to the statement. At that point, UniCredit would hold around 50% of the voting rights in Commerzbank and be able to take control of the bank, it said.

Offer made in May

UniCredit made an offer for all Commerzbank shares in May, securing access to almost half of the stock in the DAX-listed group, partly indirectly through complex financial transactions.

However, ECB approval, seen as a central step, was still pending before the share swap could be completed. UniCredit's stake in Commerzbank now rises from just under 30% to almost 50%.

The ECB's banking supervision oversees the largest banks in the eurozone. Its approval comes as no surprise, as it has repeatedly made clear that it supports cross-border bank mergers in the eurozone to strengthen the EU single market.

text:
Specialist cover for art, wine and collectibles has usually involved schedules, valuations and an underwriter's sign-off. In Singapore it now takes a smartphone.

KoverNow, a digital insurance intermediary for high-value items, has added fine art, wine, whisky and collectibles to its app-based product range, underwritten by AXA XL. Collectors can get instant quotes and buy all-risk policies covering loss, theft and accidental damage worldwide. KoverNow says it has built end-to-end digital processes for each line that remove the lengthy underwriting traditionally required for these items.

The scope reaches well past paintings. Art cover extends to sculpture and antiques, while collectibles include professionally graded trading cards and sports and film memorabilia.

That matters for how the collector market has usually been insured. New collectors in Asia have typically started with lower-cost named-peril policies before moving to broader cover. KoverNow is offering all-risk protection from the first purchase.

KoverNow chief executive Stephan Kaiser (pictured) framed the move around how collectors already buy. "Collectors already buy and trade their collections digitally, from graded trading cards acquired on online marketplaces to art bought through the e-commerce platforms of auction houses," he said. "Insurance has been the one analogue step left in that process, standing between collectors and specialised protection for their passions."

AXA XL is backing the model with its specialist capacity. Rhiannon Alban-Davies, underwriting manager for Fine Art & Specie, Asia, at AXA XL, said collectors expect specialist protection "to be just as straightforward and accessible" as the way they now build their collections. She said the partnership combines KoverNow's digital platform with "AXA XL's specialist Fine Art & Specie expertise and capacity".

The tie-up began in January 2026 with digital cover for watches, jewellery and handbags. KoverNow now plans to take the partnership to Hong Kong with the same range of categories.

Distribution is the part brokers will notice. KoverNow works with luxury retailers, financial institutions and auction houses to offer cover at the point of sale, and relies on its own proprietary model to establish authenticity and valuation. For brokers handling private clients in Singapore, and soon Hong Kong, the first specialist policy a collector buys may now come through an app at the till. When those clients bring a growing collection to a broker, the term to test first is valuation: KoverNow quotes on market value drawn from its own pricing data.

text:
MiniMed has completed its separation from Medtronic, beginning operations as a fully independent publicly traded company focused on diabetes technology and insulin delivery.

The company is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol MMED. The separation ends Medtronic’s equity ownership in MiniMed and gives the company independent control over its strategy, capital allocation, product development, and operations.

As part of the separation process, Medtronic accepted 55,032,401 Medtronic ordinary shares in exchange for 252,813,348 shares of MiniMed common stock. Following completion of the exchange offer, Medtronic no longer owns an equity stake in MiniMed.

The exchange offer was 5.4 times subscribed, reflecting demand from Medtronic shareholders seeking to exchange their shares for MiniMed stock. Newly issued MiniMed shares will be credited in book-entry form to accounts maintained by the company’s transfer agent for participating shareholders whose Medtronic shares were accepted.

MiniMed enters its next phase as a standalone diabetes technology company with a portfolio spanning insulin delivery systems, continuous glucose monitors, algorithms, and mobile applications.

The company’s integrated ecosystem is designed to connect its insulin delivery and glucose monitoring technologies with software and support services. MiniMed currently serves people with diabetes across 80 countries and has operated in the diabetes care market for more than 40 years.

As an independent company, MiniMed plans to focus its resources on advancing diabetes therapies, simplifying treatment management, and developing technologies intended to reduce the daily burden associated with diabetes care.

KEY QUOTES:

“Today marks the completion of our separation from Medtronic and a significant milestone for MiniMed. We are grateful to Medtronic for its partnership and support in reaching this point. As an independent company, we have the freedom to make the decisions we believe are right for our business and the people we serve, and the responsibility to see those decisions through. Our focus now is to put that independence to work and continue advancing what is possible in diabetes care.”

text:
By Valentina Za

MILAN, Oct 15 (Reuters) - UniCredit, Italy's second-largest bank, said on Thursday that the European Central Bank had authorised it to take control of Commerzbank, after a hostile takeover offer completed in July lifted its stake in the German rival to 48%.

UniCredit needed ECB approval to take delivery of the Commerzbank shares tendered in the €45 billion offer and advance plans for what would be Europe's biggest cross-border banking deal since the global financial crisis.

UniCredit said the ECB had authorised it to cross the 30% ownership threshold in Commerzbank and "to increase its stake further without upper limits."

It added it expected to be able to take control of Commerzbank by the end of the year with around 50% of voting rights, after completing the "remaining regulatory processes and conditions" relating to its takeover bid.

The Italian bank, which has operated Bavarian lender HVB in Germany since 2005, started investing in Commerzbank more than two years ago, as UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel embarked on a takeover that several of his predecessors had also studied.

Despite stiff opposition from Commerzbank and criticism from the German government, UniCredit secured enough shares to control ordinary shareholder resolutions while remaining below the 50% threshold that would force it to buy out minority investors in the German lender's Polish unit mBank.

Orcel has told Commerzbank to adopt the strategy he has mapped out to boost profits at the Frankfurt-based bank from January, while pushing back a full merger to 2029-2030.

The veteran dealmaker has held talks with German government representatives who want Commerzbank to retain its Frankfurt headquarters, to protect jobs and to lend to German businesses.

Once in possession of the shares, Orcel has threatened to call a shareholder vote and install a new supervisory board and management at Commerzbank, without waiting for its annual general meeting next year.

(Reporting by Valentina Za; Editing by Alexander Smith and Susan Fenton)

text:
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. The companies announced on Thursday that Volvo will use three pieces of Nvidia hardware and software in its future vehicles to provide an automated driving system that can navigate urban streets and highways.

Under the expanded partnership, Volvo will combine its vehicle safety systems and engineering with Nvidia’s Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Alpamayo driving software stack, and Halos safety evaluation layer.

The Alpamayo stack is redundant and diverse, according to Ali Kani, who heads up Nvidia’s automotive division. It combines Alpamayo, a family of AI models, datasets, and simulation and development tools used to build autonomous-driving software, with classical software that uses machine learning and camera and radar perception, he said.

“The point is we run these two stacks at the same time, and we have multimodal sensors in our philosophy because it’s a safer product that way,” Kani said, adding that the open source Alpamayo software has now been downloaded by more than 650,000 developers.

Volvo didn’t reveal the value of the partnership or which vehicle model would be the first to use this new Nvidia tech stack. But Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo’s head of software development, hinted at the scale of the deal and how it represents the automaker’s evolution toward developing a full-tech stack designed for its electric vehicles as well as its plug-in hybrids and gas-powered vehicles.

“Automakers used to be very much like car-line-based development and working with various suppliers, etc. and we have completely changed and migrated into being a full-tech stack company,” Bakkenes said, adding that Volvo will start this partnership with a brand new vehicle that “will come in the not-too-near future.”

He said the first vehicle with this new Nvidia tech stack will debut within the decade, and “then of course the technology can go beyond that.”

While Volvo’s relationship with Nvidia isn’t new, the expanded partnership represents the automaker’s effort to bring the latest automated driving software to all of its vehicles — not just its EVs.

All of Volvo’s battery-electric vehicles use Nvidia’s Orin computer chip, which processes information from cameras, radar, and other sensors to help a vehicle understand its surroundings and make driving decisions.

“What we’re going to do in the future is actually standardize more on Hyperion — also from a sensor set perspective — to really open up the stack for the wider partnership with Nvidia,” Bakkenes said.

text:
As the former head of eBay and Hewlett Packard, Meg Whitman, at least at first glance, seemed like an odd choice to serve as executive chairman for Albertsons.

Grocery chains, however, have become, or are at least on the path to becoming, technology companies that happen to sell groceries. What was once a business based on having stores located near your customer base has increasingly become about operating efficiency, digital sales, and artificial intelligence (AI).

Viewed through that lens, Whitman's appointment makes more sense, and she hit the ground running during the company's second-quarter earnings call. She acknowledged technology early on in her remarks.

"We've built a strong e-commerce platform and see AI as critical to our success," she said.

Then, she dropped the hammer.

"Our performance has fallen short. Sales and earnings growth have not met our expectations. Market share trends have lagged, and despite many individual successes across the business, we're not delivering results consistent with the quality of our assets. We must turn things around," she added.

Meg Whitman plans an Albertsons turnaround

Whitman, it should be noted, is not the CEO of Albertsons. Susan Morris holds that job.

That did not stop Whitman from making it clear that major change is coming.

"The first step is to take a hard look at the business, challenge assumptions, and decide what actions create the greatest value for customers and shareholders. That includes looking at opportunities to run the core business much better by improving the operational model and decision-making," Whitman said.

The executive chairman then essentially promised cuts, although she did not offer specifics.

"It also includes improving the cost structure, reducing price for customers, and resetting priorities for improved capital allocation. We must also take a close look at our portfolio of banners, markets, assets, and businesses as well as at potential strategic actions we can take to enhance shareholder value," she added.

Whitman made it clear that the current company was not meeting her expectations.

"We must move faster to reduce costs, reinvest much of those savings into lower prices, improve the store experience for customers, grow traffic and share in core markets, drive ID sales and revenue, and improve returns for shareholders. Albertsons must become a simpler, more focused company that gets the basics right every day," she said.

Whitman essentially put the entire company on notice.

"Everything should be on the table as we figure out how Albertsons should be structured to better compete in the years ahead," she shared.

Albertsons' sales dropped

Net sales and other revenue decreased 0.1% to $18,894.7 million for the 12 weeks ended Sept. 12, 2026, from $18,915.8 million during the 12 weeks ended Sept. 6, 2025.

"This decrease was driven by a decline in identical sales of 0.8%," the company shared in its earnings release. "Pharmacy and digital remained areas of strength, with pharmacy sales continuing to grow despite ongoing Inflation Reduction Act headwinds and digital sales increasing 11% during the second quarter of fiscal 2026. The decrease in net sales and other revenue was partially offset by higher fuel sales."

Morris' comments during the earnings call suggested that cuts are coming.

"Over time, we launched a number of initiatives for good reasons and with the right intentions. Upon reflection, however, too many initiatives, processes, and layers of complexity have built up, slowing the organization and increasing the cost of running our business," she said.

More Retail:

Target tackles a frustrating problem for shoppers

America's biggest RV seller closing more stores

Costco helps members solve a key problem, but at a cost

Like her counterpart at Kroger, Gregory Foran, Morris said that costs needed to come out of the business to lower prices for customers.

"Going forward, our focus will be much narrower. Our resources will be concentrated on the right projects that most accelerate our results, and our expectations and accountability for results will be significantly higher. We must deliver more consistently for our customers. Price matters. Promotions matter. Freshness matters," she added.

Morris also said the company now plans $2 billion in cuts over three years, up from a previous goal of $1.5 billion.

Whitman has a reputation for turnarounds

While Whitman led turnaround efforts at both HP and and eBay, not everyone praised her people skills.

"Perhaps face to face over coffee or even in the boardroom, she comes off differently. But in the public spotlight, she comes off as brash and abrasive, qualities that are ill-suited for the public face of a company desperately needs a charismatic leader to inspire the folks at HP, not to mention charm the public, the press, investors, and partners," Infoworld wrote at the time of her appointment to lead HP.

Her results, however, have been strong.

"Two and a half years later, HP's turnaround is still a work in progress, but its stock has rebounded strongly since hitting bottom a year after Whitman took over, and her plan to split the iconic computer maker into two companies garnered high marks both on Wall Street and in Silicon Valley," Stanford's Graduate School of Business shared in an interview with Whitman.

Morris promises more cuts

Like Whitman, Morris made it clear that nothing at Albertsons was safe.

"Finally, we're taking a disciplined look at our portfolio. Albertsons has strong businesses, strong banners, and valuable assets, but not all assets create the same value. Going forward, we'll be more focused," she said.

She did not specifically address closing stores, but she heavily suggested it.

"We'll invest where we have a clear path to win. "We'll exit areas that are underperforming," she added.

text:
California-based Agilent Technologies, an analytical and clinical laboratory technologies company, recently entered into a definitive agreement to purchase Philadelphia-based Proscia, a digital pathology software provider, for $240 million in cash and up to an additional $30 million based on achieving future performance milestones.

The companies previously entered into a multi-year distribution agreement in 2022 to offer a comprehensive digital diagnostic-pathology system. The purchase of Proscia will provide Agilent with multiple strategic and financial benefits including strengthening Agilent’s existing leadership in pathology instrumentation and reagents, combining AI-enabled synergies with Agilent’s companion diagnostics business, and adding a high-growth, high-margin software business to Agilent’s pathology portfolio.

“This agreement with Agilent marks an exciting milestone for Proscia and reflects the strength of the platform our team has built,” David West, Proscia co-founder and CEO, said. “Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions. Together, we can accelerate innovation while continuing to provide customers with the flexibility they need across clinical and life-sciences workflows. I am grateful to the entire Proscia team, whose dedication made this milestone possible, and look forward to building on our work as part of Agilent.”

The deal is expected to close early in Agilent’s fiscal year 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.

text:

Interest in the future of data center infrastructure is so high that the organizer of this week's OCP Global Summit in Silicon Valley said it has reached “maximum capacity” and would refuse entry for anyone not registered, even those who already booked travel.

With a record 15,000 people reportedly attending the event organized by the Meta-founded Open Compute Project, major semiconductor companies Intel, AMD and Nvidia showed off how they will power future AI data centers with new disclosures, many of which are based around the standardized server specifications championed by OCP.

[Related: How Intel’s AI Chip Strategy Is Coming Into Shape After Years Of Struggles]

These disclosures included new details for Intel’s upcoming air-cooled data center GPU, new server racks packing more than 46,000 cores’ worth of Intel Xeon CPUs, a new flexible server rack reference design from AMD, the first AMD EPYC CPU to include an LPDDR memory interface as well as open-source and Vera Rubin news from Nvidia.

Some of these announcements were aimed at partners and customers building data centers for agentic AI workloads, especially when it came to the CPU-related news because of how important the processor type has become for enabling such applications. Others, on the other hand, are meant to help with the broader AI data center buildout.

While Nvidia is far ahead of Intel and AMD in the AI infrastructure market in terms of revenue, all three companies are needed to help channel partners fulfill the ongoing buildout of AI data centers, according to Bob Venero, CEO of Fort Lauderdale, Fla.-based solution provider Future Tech Enterprise, which ranked No. 90 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500.

“The channel needs AMD, Intel and Nvidia to continue to push the limits,” he said.

Though hyperscalers and neoclouds are building much of the data center capacity to support agentic AI right now, Venero sees a huge opportunity for the channel to help enterprises secure their own infrastructure due to security and cost concerns.

“Customers are definitely figuring this out because they spent a ton of money and blew through their token budgets because they let [AI] agents run unregulated within their organizations,” he said. “So you’re seeing customers now more looking at, ‘Hey, how do we control costs? How do we drive these agents internally that will use our internal models and do things that are not necessarily cloud-based but on-prem?’”

What follows are the most important details from these six big OCP 2026 announcements.

Intel Details 480-GB D-Series GPU For Air-Cooled Servers

Intel revealed that its upcoming 480-GB “Crescent Island” data center GPU for AI inference will be known as the Intel GPU D-series and feature up to 1.3 petaflops of 8-bit floating-point compute within a 350-watt power envelope.

The chipmaker said that the D-series GPU, which is sampling with customers now, will come in a standard, air-cooled PCIe form factor that will make it easy to slot into existing data centers, with up to eight PCIe cards per server.

Intel said it’s working with a “broad ecosystem” of OEMs, ODMs, neoclouds, ISVs, appliance providers and AI-native companies to bring the GPU D-series into production. These vendors include Asus, Cisco, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, Supermicro, NetApp, Nutanix, IBM-owned Red Hat and Broadcom-owned VMware.

The GPU D-series represents Intel’s latest attempt to gain a foothold in the AI accelerator chip market after previous efforts, including its Gaudi line of chips, failed to catch traction. The new product makes use of the company’s new Xe3P architecture, which stems from the Xe architecture it began developing for client and server GPUs several years ago.

The semiconductor giant said the GPU D-series is designed for large language models, long-context workloads and concurrent services, with a single card supporting models with up to 300 billion parameters and an 8-GPU system supporting up to 1 trillion parameters.

The new product line is set to go head-to-head with Nvidia’s RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, which features 2 petaflops of 8-bit floating-point compute (FP8), 4 petaflops of 4-bit floating-point compute (FP4) and 96 GB of GDDR7 memory in a PCIe form factor that can be configured to consume up to 600 watts.

While Nvidia does not divulge the difference in performance between the air- and liquid-cooled versions of the RTX Pro 6000 on its website, a head-to-head comparison of public specifications to the Intel GPU D-series puts the former card ahead in terms of FP8 performance and offering FP4 support, which can help applications run faster.

The GPU D-series, however, packs far more memory, 480 GB, with roughly the same memory bandwidth at 1.5 TBps despite using LPDDR5X. And it seems to offer greater power efficiency by fitting 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute into only 350 watts.

Intel said the GPU D-series falls in line with its strategy to offer open systems and software architecture that allows developers to easily deploy workloads on the right hardware.

New Intel Xeon Server Racks Pack 46,000 CPU Cores For Agentic AI

Intel showed off new server rack designs that can pack more 46,000 cores’ worth of the company’s Xeon 6+ CPUs for agentic AI workloads.

These rack designs come from server vendors such as Asus, Gigabyte and Supermicro. Many of them are based on the Open Compute Project’s Open Rack v3 standard to, in Intel’s words, “simplify deployment and integration within open data center infrastructure.”

The semiconductor giant made the display as it experiences a surge in demand for CPUs due to the meteoric rise of agentic AI workloads in data centers.

The server racks at the OCP Global Summit were designed with high densities of CPUs to “orchestrate workloads, process data, manage I/O and execute tasks that keep” accelerator chips such as GPUs running at full speed,” the chipmaker said.

In some configurations, these server racks can fit more than 46,000 cores from Intel’s Xeon 6+ processors in a rack power envelope of 133.45 kilowatts, according to the company.

Launched over the summer, the Xeon 6+ processors, code-named “Clearwater Forest,” feature up to 288 efficiency cores in a 450-watt power envelope.

AMD Reveals Flexible ‘Helion’ Server Rack Design For Agentic AI

AMD revealed a flexible server rack reference design called “Helion” that enables partners to customize compute needs for customers running agentic AI workloads.

Calling Helion an “open blueprint,” the chip designer said it’s based on an Open Compute Project spec-design that can use EPYC CPUs and Instinct GPUs—or just the CPUs.

AMD said server vendors plan to release Helion rack configurations starting this November. Supporting vendors include Cisco, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro.

It’s yet another move by AMD to challenge Nvidia’s dominance of the AI infrastructure market and keep the pressure on other rivals such as Intel, particularly as agentic AI workloads creates unprecedented demand for CPUs.

The idea with Helion is to let customers “match CPU performance, core density and power with GPU acceleration for the work their AI agents perform,” AMD said.

This means customers can create “virtually any configuration” to meet their workload requirements, and this includes options for liquid- and air-cooled versions of Helion.

For instance, AMD said a CPU-only rack with 6th-Gen EPYC processors can pack up to 32,768 cores for hyperscalers that need “dedicated capacity for agent execution and connections to separate model inference infrastructure.”

Helion can also enable an all-in-one rack that brings together “AMD EPYC CPU nodes, AMD Instinct MI350P GPU nodes and general-purpose compute on one platform” for enterprise customers running agentic AI workloads, according to the company.

Nvidia Open-Sources Run:ai, Other AI Data Center Software

Nvidia said it has made software components for various aspects of running AI data centers, including Run:ai, available under open-source licenses.

The vendor said it’s open-sourcing these software components as part of its DSX AI Factory platform, which brings together software libraries, workflow guides and reference designs to help partners and customers maximize tokens per watt in AI data centers.

The push is part of Nvidia’s strategy to provide a “vertically integrated” platform that is “horizontally open,” which has become a common line by the company this year.

The most notable move is with Run:ai, the Kubernetes-based workload management and orchestration software that Nvidia acquired for a reported $700 million in late 2024.

When Nvidia announced the acquisition earlier that year, the company said it planned to use Run:ai to boost its DGX Cloud, which launched in 2023 as a full-stack commercial service that was meant to simplify AI training in public cloud environments.

However, the company switched gears in late 2025 when it reportedly restructured the DGX Cloud business and shifted its focus to an “internal cloud environment for building and operating AI,” as Nvidia’s web page for DGX Cloud now says.

With the open-source move, Nvidia said, “it is now possible for every NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner and AI cloud to increase workload throughput, improve GPU utilization, and operate shared AI infrastructure more efficiently and effectively.”

This involves making available the full Run:ai platform as well as individual components: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management and Workload Map. Partners and customers can determine whether to adopt the full platform, use it to build their own products or integrate individual components, according to Nvidia.

Outside of Run:ai, the company said it open-sourced software components for “configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal.”

These components, originally designed for DGX Cloud, consist of Nvidia Config Manager, Nvidia Cluster Readiness Engine, Nvidia Rack Management Service and Cluster API Provider for Nvidia Infrastructure Controller.

With the software components, Nvidia said, cloud providers and software partners can “integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms.”

text:
US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.

It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.

A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.

The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department.

Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”

News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executives Jes Staley and his links to Epstein.

Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American banker resigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan.

The Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were “indeed close” and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”.

Staley was eventually banned from the UK’s financial sector in 2023 for playing down those ties, and failed to overturn that decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year.

That included Staley admitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staff in New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchange referring to Disney princesses, in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing.

After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”.

In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”.

Barclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient.

The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”.

“This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”.

Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.”

Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.

title: As Medicare's new ACO model begins, kidney care cannot be left behind
authors: Keith A. Bellovich, D.O., MBA, Mary Dittrich, M.D., FASN, Jeffrey Giullian, M.D., MBA, Carney Taylor, M.D., MBA, Heather Trafton, MBA, Keith A. Bellovich, D.O, Mary Dittrich, M.D, Jeffrey Giullian

text:
© Jo Panuwat D - stock.adobe.com

In 2027, Medicare will enter an important transition in its continued evolution toward accountable care. The Long-term Enhanced Accountable Care Organization Design (LEAD) Model will begin a 10-year test intended to make accountable care more stable, inclusive and responsive to patients with complex needs.

Additionally, next year the Comprehensive Kidney Care Contracting (CKCC) Model, Medicare’s principal accountable care model for people with advanced kidney disease, is scheduled to sunset. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) has not announced whether accountable kidney care will continue through an extension, a successor model or a defined specialty track within LEAD.

The parallel timing of LEAD and CKCC allows CMS to preserve and strengthen accountable kidney care, just as LEAD builds on lessons from nearly 15 years of primary care-based accountable care models. As CMS designs the next generation of accountable care, it must preserve a dedicated model for kidney care. The clinical improvements achieved through CKCC, combined with CMS’s recent financial reforms, make a strong case for building on the model. Allowing it to end without a successor risks losing the clinical infrastructure and provider investments built over the life of the model.

Keith Bellovich, D.O., MBA

Mary Dittrich, M.D., FASN

Jeffrey Giullian, M.D., MBA

Carney Taylor, M.D., MBA

Heather Trafton, MBA

Patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) are among Medicare’s most clinically complex beneficiaries. They frequently live with multiple chronic conditions, experience 1.5 hospitalizations per person-year, and require intensive care coordination across providers and care settings.

As a result, this population generates outsized cost for the health care system. According to the United States Renal Data System (USRDS), the cost of care for the 3.8 million Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) beneficiaries living with CKD increased to $141.1 billion in 2023, accounting for 36% of total 2023 costs. The yearly per-person cost for Medicare FFS beneficiaries who live with CKD was more than $31,000 in 2023, according to USRDS, about 2.5 times the cost for Medicare FFS beneficiaries without CKD, diabetes or heart failure. For Medicare FFS beneficiaries receiving in-center hemodialysis, annual spending averaged more than $103,000 per person in 2023, according to USRDS.

Despite the need for higher levels of care and more coordination, traditional FFS payment models do not reliably support the interdisciplinary teams, patient education, clinical analytics, medication management, transition planning and continuous outreach necessary to coordinate this complex care. Today, nearly half of patients with Stage 4-5 CKD do not see a nephrologist, and up to 70% begin dialysis unexpectedly in an acute setting, according to USRDS, leading to poorer outcomes and significantly higher Medicare spending.

CKCC was designed to address this fragmentation in care. Kidney Contracting Entities bring nephrologists together with transplant providers and, in many cases, kidney care organizations and other partners. They invest in care coordination and accept accountability for the quality and total cost of their patients’ care. Unlike a model built primarily around a patient’s relationship with a primary care practice, CKCC recognizes that as kidney disease advances, the nephrologist is frequently the principal clinician managing the patient’s care, with the expertise to drive improved outcomes.

The model is working. CKCC encourages organizations to develop interventions tailored to the kidney disease continuum, such as slowing progression where possible, preparing patients for dialysis before a crisis occurs, increasing the uptake of home dialysis, improving access to kidney transplantation and educating patients to make informed decisions about their care.

The second independent evaluation of the model, released earlier this year, found significant improvements across several measures closely linked to patients’ experiences and outcomes. Optimal starts to treatment for ESRD increased by 31%. Home dialysis increased by 10%, home dialysis training increased by 22%, and preemptive transplant waitlisting increased by 37%. Patients in the model also reported receiving more information about their treatment options, while patient activation scores improved over time.

Kidney care needs a dedicated place in accountable care

The CMS Innovation Center now faces a consequential choice about the future of specialty-led accountable care. LEAD creates new opportunities to integrate specialists into accountable care, but it remains organized around primary care.

One of those tools is CMS-Administered Risk Arrangements (CARA), a voluntary LEAD initiative that allows accountable care organizations (ACOs) to establish episode-based risk arrangements with specialty providers. Through CARA, ACOs and specialists can negotiate target prices for defined episodes of care and share accountability for their cost and performance.

CARA could strengthen specialist participation in accountable care, but it is not a substitute for a kidney-specific model built around longitudinal, nephrologist-led accountability. Patients with advanced kidney disease require sustained management across CKD, dialysis, transplantation and supportive care — not accountability limited to individual episodes of care.

A specialist arrangement within a broader ACO may complement that work, but it does not necessarily replicate the focused accountability, clinical expertise and care coordination that CKCC was designed to provide. As kidney disease progresses, nephrologists often become the clinicians most responsible for treatment decisions, care coordination and patient outcomes.

As CMS shapes the next generation of accountable care, it should determine how to preserve a model for accountable kidney care, whether through a dedicated successor model, a clearly defined track within LEAD where patients align through nephrologists, or an extension of CKCC while a longer-term approach is developed.

CKCC’s early results do not tell the whole story

By law, the Innovation Center must design models that either generate savings for Medicare, improve quality or — ideally — both. But formal evaluations, like those for all but a handful of models CMS has tested, have found that the models have resulted in a net increase in Medicare spending after accounting for incentive payments. The most recent evaluation found CKCC increased net Medicare spending by an estimated $275 million in 2023.

CMS responded to the model’s early spending results by making substantial changes beginning in 2026. The agency increased benchmark discounts, reduced the CKD Quarterly Capitation Payment, eliminated the kidney transplant bonus and extended CKCC through 2027. CMS stated these changes were intended to improve the model’s financial performance while preserving its quality gains.

An independent actuarial analysis by Wakely Consulting Group illustrates how consequential those changes may be. Wakely applied the 2026 payment policies retrospectively to historical financial data. It estimated that the revised policies would have reduced total model payments by approximately 45% in 2023 and 40% in 2024. Under that counterfactual analysis, the model would have generated an estimated $26 million in net savings to CMS in 2023 and $90 million in 2024. Those potential net savings jump to $112 million and $118 million in 2023 and 2024, respectively, if current model participants were in full-risk tracks. Those findings tell us that policy makers should not rely solely on financial results from a model design that CMS has already substantially revised.

The Wakely analysis also reinforces a key lesson from Medicare payment reform. Accountable care models rarely reach their full potential immediately. Building clinical infrastructure, integrating data, changing practice patterns and engaging patients takes time. The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), for example, did not generate cumulative net savings for CMS until its fifth year, yet has since produced substantial and sustained savings. In 2024 alone, MSSP generated more than $6.6 billion in savings and returned $2.5 billion back to CMS. CKCC deserves the same opportunity to mature under its revised financial structure before a final judgment is made about its long-term value.

A road map for the future

A successor could take several forms: an additional extension of CKCC, a refined kidney-specific model or a dedicated specialty track within LEAD. Whatever form the next model takes, its design should preserve the progress already made while addressing the operational and financial barriers that could undermine long-term participation.

First, CMS should expand access for patients and nephrologists. Model participation should be managed at the tax identification number level, consistent with LEAD, while allowing providers in hospital systems, multispecialty groups and academic institutions to seek exceptions when overlap rules would otherwise prevent participation.

Beneficiary alignment should similarly reflect how kidney care is delivered. A 12-month look-back based on qualifying nephrology services would create a clearer and more current connection between patients and participating providers. CMS should also establish an appropriate pathway for patients with Stage 3B CKD, when education, medication management and earlier intervention are critical to delay progression.

Second, the financial methodology must accurately reflect the complexity and changing health status of the population. Patients with Stage 4 or 5 CKD and ESRD should be treated as high-needs beneficiaries, with a consistent concurrent risk-adjustment methodology that captures disease progression and changes in treatment status during the year.

Benchmarks and trends should also be based on the populations served. Spending trends for patients with late-stage CKD should reflect their experiences, not those of the broader Medicare population. CMS should avoid policies that punish organizations for savings they have already produced, preserve prior savings and maintain advance shared savings payments that support up-front investment. Benchmark discounts should be limited to 3%, with the discount for ESRD applied only to nondialysis spending, as dialysis costs are largely nondiscretionary and difficult for participants to influence.

Third, quality accountability should be meaningful, predictable and proportionate. CMS should reduce the quality withhold to 3%, consistent with LEAD. Kidney care measures frequently involve small denominators and year-to-year variation that may not reflect genuine differences in care. A smaller, better-targeted withholding would preserve a strong incentive for improvement without making financial performance excessively dependent on statistical volatility.

The model should focus on three or four measures that participants can understand and influence. Optimal Starts and the Patient Activation Measure should remain central and be supported by more timely data and clearer calculation methods. A hospitalization or readmission measure could also be appropriate if benchmarked against comparable kidney populations and incorporating kidney-specific acuity.

Finally, CMS should evaluate the model that exists today, not only the version that operated in its earliest years. Formal evaluations should continue to report observed results in accordance with the policies in place during each performance year. But CMS should also publicly reassess earlier years using the major design changes now governing CKCC, including reduced capitation payments, stronger savings guarantees, elimination of transplant bonuses, changes to skin substitute payment and the removal of providers that have exited the model. This would help policy makers distinguish between the effects of specialty-led care delivery and the consequences of an early payment design that CMS has already changed.

Together, these refinements would create a model or track that is easier to enter, more stable to operate, more accurate in measuring financial performance and more focused on outcomes that matter to patients.

Build on what Medicare has begun

CKCC has demonstrated that specialty-focused accountability can change how kidney care is delivered. Patients are more likely to begin dialysis under optimal conditions, use home dialysis, receive earlier consideration for a transplant and obtain information that helps them make consequential decisions about their care.

CMS has already revised the features most responsible for the model’s early net spending. The rational next step is to assess those changes, preserve the clinical infrastructure that has been built and establish a stable long-term program for accountable kidney care.

Medicare is designing the next generation of accountable care. Patients with advanced kidney disease — and the specialists who care for them — must have a clear place in it.

Keith Bellovich, D.O., MBA, is the chief nephrologist at Strive Health and a nationally recognized voice in kidney care advocacy and quality improvement.

Mary Dittrich, M.D., FASN, is chief medical officer and executive vice president of U.S. Renal Care as well as co-founder and partner of Boise Kidney and Hypertension Institute.

Jeffrey Giullian, M.D., MBA, serves as chief medical officer of DaVita Kidney Care.

Carney Taylor, M.D., MBA, brings more than 25 years of clinical experience as a leading nephrologist to his role as chief medical officer at Interwell Health.

Heather Trafton, MBA, is CEO of Evergreen Nephrology.
