text:
AstraZeneca adds an AI discovery partner for liver and heart disease, with $40 million upfront and no efficacy or safety data yet reported. Credit: Stock.Adobe.com/Askar

AstraZeneca has signed a drug discovery collaboration and licensing agreement with insitro to apply artificial intelligence (AI) to target identification and therapeutic design in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and cardiomyopathies, the companies announced Oct. 15.1,2 Insitro will receive $40 million upfront and is eligible for up to approximately $1.46 billion in milestones.1,2

Sharon Barr, executive vice president and head of BioPharmaceuticals research and development at AstraZeneca, tied the agreement to target selection: “We know that disease biology is incredibly complex, and one of the most critical decisions in R&D is selecting the right target. This strategic collaboration underscores our commitment to maximizing the potential of cutting-edge AI to tackle the root cause of disease. Partnering with insitro, we will use advanced AI to identify the biological drivers of disease to support the rapid discovery of high-quality novel targets, advancing our ambition to deliver the next generation of medicines to patients faster.”1

“MASH and cardiomyopathies are prevalent, underdiagnosed diseases where high-content data holds immense potential for uncovering disease drivers. By applying AI to these complex datasets, we can unlock greater discovery power and reveal novel genetic insights.”

What are AstraZeneca and insitro agreeing to do?

Insitro will use its Virtual Human platform to identify causal disease biology in both indications and advance AstraZeneca-nominated targets from discovery to development candidate.1,2 The platform combines large-scale human and cellular data with AI-enabled target identification and medicine design.1

AstraZeneca will take the clinical development and regulatory work and holds exclusive worldwide rights to the selected programs; insitro’s release adds that AstraZeneca will also lead commercialization.1,2

Beyond the upfront payment, insitro is eligible for single-digit royalties on global sales.1,2 The two releases describe the milestones slightly differently: AstraZeneca cites development and commercial milestones, while insitro includes discovery milestones.1,2

The upfront payment represents less than 3% of the combined headline value, and neither company disclosed the number of targets, program timelines or payment schedule.

Why are MASH and cardiomyopathies difficult to treat?

Insitro’s release says each disease is defined by heterogeneity, with a single diagnostic label covering patients whose underlying biology differs, which has complicated treatment.2

Daphne Koller, Ph.D., founder and CEO of insitro, said: “MASH and cardiomyopathies are prevalent, underdiagnosed diseases where high-content data holds immense potential for uncovering disease drivers. By applying AI to these complex datasets, we can unlock greater discovery power and reveal novel genetic insights. Our platform simultaneously deconvolutes disease biology and identifies causal drivers of disease pathologies. Partnering with AstraZeneca allows us to pair our deep biological precision with their pharmaceutical expertise and scale with potential for accelerated advancement of novel programs through development and to patients.”2

In MASH, the treatment landscape has changed recently. The FDA approved resmetirom (Rezdiffra) in March 2024 under its accelerated approval pathway for adults with noncirrhotic disease and moderate to advanced liver scarring, to be used with diet and exercise. The agency, which at the time referred to the condition as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, said patients had previously lacked a medication that directly addressed their liver damage, and cited an estimate of 6 million to 8 million U.S. patients at that disease stage.3

The cardiomyopathy picture is less defined in the releases, which do not specify which forms are in scope. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the most common inherited cardiovascular disorder, is estimated to affect 1 in 500 people, and a published review notes that existing studies may have underestimated its prevalence.4

That offers one illustration of the underdiagnosis Koller describes, though it should not be read as the collaboration’s target population.

How does the collaboration fit each company’s portfolio?

AstraZeneca describes cardiovascular, renal and metabolism as one of its main disease areas and a key growth driver, with an emphasis on the links among the heart, kidneys, liver and pancreas.1 A program spanning a liver disease and heart muscle diseases fits within that framing.

Insitro says it has built a multimodal corpus of human and cellular data since 2018 and is advancing nine programs, including genetic regulators of liver fat and fibrosis expected to enter the clinic in early 2027.2 The company reports more than $750 million in capital and existing collaborations with Bristol Myers Squibb, Lilly and Gilead.2

The release does not say how its internal liver programs relate to targets AstraZeneca will nominate.

What remains unknown about the collaboration?

No candidate, efficacy data or safety data accompany the announcement, and the collaboration sits at the discovery stage. Targets identified through AI-driven analysis of human data will still need validation through preclinical work and clinical trials, where heterogeneity of disease could also affect trial design.

Milestone and royalty figures are potential payments contingent on progress that neither company has timed publicly. Neither release addresses market reaction, and independent verification of the platform’s performance in these indications was not available at the time of publication.

title: Microsoft's CEO is still haunted by staying silent in a meeting with Bill Gates | Fortune

But rather than challenge the proposal, he sat through the review without voicing his concerns.

text:
Nadella recalled a meeting in around 2008-2009 called by then-chairman Bill Gates to review a potential acquisition involving a team working on parallel data warehousing. Nadella, who was leading Microsoft’s search engine team at the time, thought the deal made little sense.

“I looked at it, [and thought], it is completely architecturally stupid in that time to go buy that,” Nadella said on an episode of the Confession with Ali Partovi podcast released this week. But rather than challenge the proposal, he sat through the review without voicing his concerns.

“It haunts me to think that I may be in a review where there’s somebody in that meeting who sees the future a lot more clearly than I do and the other person presenting—but does not really advocate for it,” Nadella said. “And so that’s what I did.”

He left the meeting thinking it had been a “waste of time.” In hindsight, however, the experience became a reminder of how easy it can be to stay quiet rather than challenge a decision—even when you believe speaking up could lead to a better outcome.

How Steve Ballmer taught Satya Nadella to voice concerns

Nadella admitted that voicing dissent can be difficult at any company, especially one as large as Microsoft. But a conversation with then-Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer helped shape his view of leadership: Employees should think beyond their individual responsibilities and take an “owner mindset,” considering what’s best for the company as a whole.

“Life’s not lived by just being so transactional about everything,” Nadella said. “Because at the end of the day, we all perish, and nobody’s going to look at any balance sheet or income statement. It’s going to be like, hey, ‘How do you live your life?’”

In other words, career success isn’t just about checking off boxes or avoiding conflict. It’s about having the courage to stand up for what you believe is right and helping the company make better decisions—even when that means challenging your colleagues. The key, Nadella said, is learning how to push for the right outcome without putting others on the defensive.

And now that he’s leading the $4 trillion giant, Nadella’s building a culture where employees can consistently speak up and push for the best possible outcome remains a challenge.

“To create an environment in which somebody feels like, ‘Wow, I always want to go for the global maxima’—and to have that be a cultural norm is a tough thing to orchestrate.”

Reed Hastings and Ray Dalio say disagreeing at work isn’t disloyal—it’s essential for success

The ability to respectfully challenge a colleague or boss is a trait many business leaders value—but fostering that kind of candor takes deliberate effort.

Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings has acknowledged that disagreeing with a boss or coworker doesn’t come naturally to most people. At Netflix, however, managers are encouraged to “farm for dissent” among employees.

“To disagree silently is disloyal,” Hastings said in 2024.

Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio has a similar philosophy, boiling the principle down to a simple rule: “Speak up, own it, or get out.”

“Just like everything else, principles need to be questioned and debated,” Dalio wrote. “What you’re not allowed to do is complain and criticize privately– either to others or in your own head. If you can’t fulfill this obligation, then you must go.

Former PepsiCo CEO Indra Nooyi has offered a practical way for leaders to make sure dissenting voices are heard: actively invite them into the conversation.

“At the end of the meeting, the person who is the head of the table should always go around and ask everybody else, ‘Do you have anything else to add,” so that any quiet voices are allowed to speak up,” Nooyi said in a MasterClass course.

“It’s very, very important because sometimes people just feel like they’re not going to be heard, or people talk over them.”

description:

text:
With today's launch of NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, we're collaborating with NVIDIA to help enterprises customize Nemotron open models for the work that matters most to them. We've had early access to the model and have been post-training it ahead of the launch with enterprises like Skydance and EY.

Starting today, this service is available to any enterprise through Scale Post-Training, a new offering within Scale GenAI Portfolio that helps enterprises customize leading open-weight models, including Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and the full Nemotron open model family. Post-training teaches an existing model a particular job using examples of that job done well, turning a general-purpose model into a specialist. For Nemotron, we combine our evaluation methodology, data and training expertise with NVIDIA post-training tools, so enterprises can balance cost, performance and control in building agentic systems and workflows that run natively in their environments.

This collaboration advances our mission to develop reliable AI systems for the world's most important decisions. For more than a decade, our data and evaluations have helped train the world's leading AI models. Now, we're bringing that same work to enterprises customizing open-weight models.

Turning Open Models Into Enterprise Specialists

The question for enterprises is no longer which model is best in general. It's which model is best for a specific job, at a sustainable cost and speed for the business. At production volume, inference costs add up quickly. Deployments will increasingly combine multiple models of different sizes, modalities, providers, strengths and costs, and open-weight models are a growing part of that mix – especially when paired with expert post-training in service of a specific use case or workflow. They can run inside a company's own infrastructure and be tuned to specific tasks, which gives enterprises more control over quality, cost and where their data is processed.

“Open models give enterprises a head start on building with their own data and intelligence,” said Joey Conway, senior director of Nemotron Models and Software at NVIDIA. “With NVIDIA Nemotron open weights, datasets and post-training tools, Scale AI is creating specialized models that boost accuracy with custom business intelligence, powering efficient systems of models for advanced agentic systems and workflows.”

"NVIDIA is giving enterprises open models they can actually make their own, and Nemotron is a big step forward,” said Francis deSouza, CEO of Scale AI. “The future of enterprise AI is multi-model, and the advantage will go to organizations that can prove which model is best for each job. With NVIDIA, Skydance and EY, we’re showing that with Scale Post-Training, an open-weight model can match or outperform the models enterprises run today at a fraction of the cost."

Every general-purpose model – open-weight or closed – starts as a generalist that doesn't know a company's policies, terminology or workflows. Closing these gaps takes more than access to the weights. Someone has to define what "correct" means for each workflow through a representative evaluation dataset, build the data that teaches the model and prove the system is ready for production. This is the work Scale does. We measure the model a customer runs today on tasks from their own workflow, build training and evaluation data for that workflow, find the right post-training recipe, post-train Nemotron with NVIDIA's open tools and test each version inside the same agent workflow it will run in production. Along the way, our engineers contribute improvements back to those tools for the open-source community. Read more about our NVIDIA partnership here.

Enterprises Building With Nemotron

With Skydance, we’re using Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to automate a core finance workflow. The agent reviews vendor credit memos, statements and invoices, many of them scanned, and matches them against the company’s financial records to find credits it’s owed. Tested on real tickets from the production workflow, Nemotron post-trained by Scale matched the accuracy of the frontier model Skydance runs in production today, at about 40x lower inference cost and 5x faster response times.

With EY, we’re building a due diligence agent that answers deal questions by finding and reconciling information across the hundreds of files in an M&A virtual data room. In evaluations across hundreds of questions from held-out data rooms, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL post-trained by Scale matched the accuracy of the frontier model EY uses today, at about one-eighteenth of the inference cost and with answers returned more than twice as fast.

We're also working with a global insurance company on a copilot that helps customer service representatives during live French-language roadside assistance calls, where getting the answer right the first time builds customer trust and keeps costs in check. The copilot pulls out the key facts of each case, recommends the benefits the customer's policy covers and flags when a representative might promise something that policy doesn't include. In controlled evaluations, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with Scale Post-Training was up to 31 percentage points more accurate than the model the company uses in production today, at about a quarter of the inference cost. Learn more about this in our technical blog.

text:
Deloitte has launched Risk Clarity, an AI-native solution designed to support organisations across the enterprise risk life cycle through agentic capabilities.

The offering is delivered through Ascend, Deloitte’s AI-enabled service delivery platform.

Risk Clarity aims to improve consistency, clarity and visibility across enterprise processes, risks and controls, while reducing manual work.

It includes six modules and more than 25 agents covering automated testing, control optimisation, issue management, key risk indicators, process mapping, reporting and risk assessment.

Deloitte said the platform gives clients a single point of access to its industry experience, proprietary data, agentic workflows and alliance technologies.

It can be used throughout the delivery life cycle, from strategy and design to programme management, code generation, data validation and testing.

The company said organisations can use Risk Clarity to replace fragmented and manual risk activities with a more connected, agile and data-driven operating model.

Deloitte Global and US Regulatory, Risk and Forensic leader Gina Primeaux said: “Organisations are under growing pressure to understand risk clearly, act faster, and do so across increasingly complex environments.

“Risk Clarity brings together Deloitte’s deep risk experience, AI-powered intelligence and a modular set of capabilities to help clients modernise how they manage, execute and oversee risk across the enterprise.”

The company added that the modules allow organisations to start with selected use cases and scale deployment over time.

The capabilities include translating regulations into actionable requirements; linking process documentation directly with risks, regulations and controls; and automating risk identification alongside effectiveness scoring.

They also cover reviewing and rationalising controls, automating control testing, and supporting issue creation, early data-quality detection and thematic root-cause analysis.

Human-in-the-loop validation remains part of the process, allowing risk teams to focus on higher-value work and more informed decision-making.

text:
Agilent Technologies, announced on October 13, 2026 that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Proscia, a Philadelphia-based provider of digital pathology software for clinical and life sciences customers. The all-cash transaction is valued at $240 million at closing, with up to an additional $30 million based on achieving future performance milestones.

“Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market,” said Agilent President and CEO Padraig McDonnell. “The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use. With Proscia’s leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data.”

A Central Operating Layer for Digital Pathology

Proscia’s software platform serves as a central operating layer for digital pathology, connecting slide scanners, laboratory information systems, image-analysis applications, AI tools, people, and data so customers can manage images, data, and workflows in one environment. The company serves more than 4,000 laboratories, hospitals, and clinics, as well as 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies, with trailing 12-month revenue exceeding $18 million. Its platform holds FDA 510(k) clearance for primary diagnosis.

“This agreement with Agilent marks an exciting milestone for Proscia and reflects the strength of the platform our team has built,” said David West, Co-Founder and CEO of Proscia. “Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions. Together, we can accelerate innovation while continuing to provide customers with the flexibility they need across clinical and life-sciences workflows. I am grateful to the entire Proscia team, whose dedication made this milestone possible, and look forward to building on our work as part of Agilent.”

From Partners to One Company

The acquisition builds on a multi-year distribution agreement Agilent and Proscia signed in September 2022 to offer a comprehensive digital diagnostic pathology system. It also follows Agilent’s recently completed transaction with Biocare Medical. Agilent says the deal will:

Strengthen its pathology portfolio: Agilent’s pathology instruments and reagents will be paired with Proscia’s vendor-agnostic digital pathology platform and established customer base.

Enhance companion diagnostics and drug discovery offerings: Proscia’s growing repository of real-world data offers AI-enabled synergies with Agilent’s companion diagnostics business, adding value for biopharma partners and clinical and translational research customers.

Support long-term growth: Proscia’s recurring-revenue software model adds a high-growth, high-margin business to Agilent’s pathology portfolio.

The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and is expected to close early in Agilent’s fiscal year 2027. Proscia will then become part of Agilent’s Life Sciences and Diagnostics Markets Group.

About Proscia

Proscia is a Philadelphia-based pathology AI company rewiring pathology for precision medicine across drug discovery, development, and diagnosis. Its Concentriq platform brings intelligence to the scientists, pathologists, and laboratory leaders behind the most critical decisions in medicine, helping more breakthroughs reach the patients they were made for. Proscia is trusted by 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies and was named Global 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology in Europe.

text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the chipmaker “absolutely must” work with Chinese AI companies on monitoring risks around the “potentially dangerous” technology.

“We absolutely should work with each other so that we advance the technology safely,” he told CNBC during a media briefing on Wednesday evening in London.

Discussions around AI safety have intensified in recent months, after researchers from AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic called for a slowdown on developing the tech and warned of existential risks to humanity.

While OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei have called for greater regulation, Huang has emerged as a prominent voice in opposition to that view.

Huang said that “dialogue” was the way to work with Chinese AI companies, adding that he has “dialogues with many of the researchers in China.”

“We ought to enhance the dialogue,” he added. “The United States should do it... I advocated that the U.K. do the same thing.”

AI safety has become a key topic between the U.S. and Chinese governments, with both countries weighing how to address the risks posed by the rapidly advancing tech.

Prior to U.S. President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed the prospect of a “U.S.-China AI dialogue” with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, in September, including a channel for incidents “up to a national security level.”

A Chinese readout of the meeting said President Xi pointed out that China and the U.S. “may have competition, but they may cooperate even more” in AI. “The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” Xi said, per the readout.

Huang said that the U.K. is in a position “in the world to be able to be a convener of many of these dialogues” related to AI, because of the country’s “intellectual capital.”

David Vaillant has been a lawyer, a central banker, a dealmaker and a professor. Now he has a new job: finding roughly $1.5bn of investor money every week.

That is the pace at which the World Bank Group’s three main lending arms, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), the International Development Association (IDA), and the International Finance Corporation (IFC) raised funds in the 2026 financial year, totalling nearly $82bn from international capital markets. As the group’s new Managing Director and Chief Financial Officer, announced on 8 October, Vaillant will run that global funding machine. Alongside its own borrowing, President Ajay Banga wants Vaillant to pull far more private money into emerging market infrastructure and energy transition projects.

Finance executives managing cross-border capital structures, debt issuances and corporate acquisitions, Vaillant’s appointment offers a useful look at how big institutions are trying to share risk with private money.

Lawyer, Central Banker, Dealmaker, Professor

Vaillant’s career trajectory covers an unusually broad set of disciplines. He began in corporate legal practice advising companies on cross-border transactions before joining the Banque de France, where he gained firsthand exposure to central banking regulation and systemic risk oversight. At BNP Paribas, his responsibilities expanded into sovereign advisory, counselling governments and central banks across both developed and developing economies. He also taught finance, sustainable finance and international macroeconomics at HEC Paris and Sciences Po.

His most prominent corporate milestone came as Global Head of Finance, Strategy and Participations at BNP Paribas Asset Management. There, Vaillant led the €5.1bn ($5.6bn) acquisition of AXA Investment Managers, a transaction that created one of Europe’s largest asset managers with approximately €1.6tr in client assets.

Banga highlighted this breadth of experience upon the appointment, noting that Vaillant has spent his career managing finance at scale while working closely with investors, governments and central banks. The modern World Bank CFO role requires a leader who can navigate complex cross-border legal frameworks, structure multi-party transactions and manage diverse public and private stakeholders simultaneously.

Balancing an $82bn Funding Program with Private Capital

The $82bn annual borrowing programed cements the World Bank’s status as one of the world’s largest supranational debt issuers. Yet public multilateral lending alone cannot close the global infrastructure financing gap, which is estimated to require trillions of dollars in annual capital allocation.

Banga’s vision does not replace traditional bond issuances; rather, it aims to use the bank’s balance sheet to attract commercial capital that currently stays on the sidelines. To achieve this, Vaillant inherits an operation tasked with making emerging market assets viable for risk-averse institutional investors like pension funds and insurance firms.

First, this requires de-risking foreign exchange and sovereign credit exposure. Tools the group already uses include political risk guarantees, first-loss equity tranches and specialized currency hedging mechanisms. By absorbing early-stage project risks, multilateral lenders lower the overall cost of capital for private co-investors who would otherwise find emerging market yields insufficient relative to the perceived risk.

Second, one priority is likely to be the standardization of blended finance assets. Private institutional investors often avoid emerging market infrastructure because individual deals are too small, fragmented and bespoke to manage efficiently. By pooling infrastructure loans into standardized, rated financial instruments, the World Bank can create tradable asset classes that global institutional investors can syndicate or purchase at scale.

Lessons for Corporate Finance Leaders

While few corporate treasurers manage an annual funding engine of $82bn, Vaillant’s background and the mandate he inherits offer practical parallels for enterprise finance strategy.

The decision to buy scale through the AXA Investment Managers acquisition rather than relying on organic growth illustrates a key lesson for corporate strategy: when market fragmentation threatens margins, aggressive consolidation can lower operating costs over time and yield capital efficiencies. Corporate CFOs evaluating strategic growth can look to large asset management consolidations as a template for building operational scale.

Furthermore, as corporate borrowing costs remain elevated compared to the prior decade, finance leaders managing heavy capital expenditure programes (particularly in energy, supply chain infrastructure and technology) can adopt multilateral co-investment techniques. Structuring joint ventures, private credit facilities or syndicated debt vehicles with institutional partners allows corporate treasurers to fund large-scale investments while sharing risk and preserving balance sheet capacity.

Lawyer, central banker, dealmaker, professor. For a CFO job in 2026, that CV no longer looks unusual.

[SAN FRANCISCO] Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang said he would halt the supply of chips to a customer that was developing unsafe artificial intelligence software, though he does not believe that the current level of concern about the technology is warranted.

“It’s a hypothetical, but yes,” he said in an interview with Bloomberg’s Emily Chang in London when asked if he would stop supplying an irresponsible developer.

“But before you do so, you would have a conversation. We don’t run other people’s companies, and there’s a limit to the judgment we apply to other companies’ use of our technology. Our technology is general-purpose.”

Nvidia is the dominant supplier of AI accelerators, the chips used to train and run AI models. That has put it at the centre of a debate over whether the software risks growing too powerful and slipping out of human control.

AI executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei have proposed an industry-wide slowdown to address the concerns.

Huang, who is on a tour through Europe ahead of a company event in Berlin, said the fears about AI safety are part of growing pains for an industry expanding quickly. The executive said he believes that the software can be controlled and deployed safely.

As part of its commitment to keeping AI safe, Nvidia is donating US$250 million over five years towards UK research into the issue.

The support will come in the form of access to time on advanced computers. Various academic institutions in that country, including the University of Oxford and University College London, will study safeguards and ways to control AI agents.

“Many of the young companies are going through growing pains, and they’re growing incredibly fast,” Huang said in the interview. “There’s an accountability, responsibility that goes along with building companies that they’re just growing into.”

Some of the concern that exists is “self-imposed”, he said, and the industry in general is doing a “horrible job” of explaining the benefits of the new technology.

AI itself can be used to safeguard and help contain the technology, Huang added.

“We should accelerate the integration of this containment technology into AI systems,” he said. “We should accelerate the development of monitoring technologies, and AI is that monitor. So we should accelerate AI technology.”

text:
Agilent Technologies Inc., is a global leader in analytical and clinical laboratory technologies, announced it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Proscia, a provider of digital pathology software for clinical and life-sciences customers, in an all-cash transaction valued at $240 million in cash at closing and up to an additional $30 million based on achieving future performance milestones.

Proscia is a leading independent provider of enterprise digital pathology software, serving as a key enabler to address emerging trends in the $5 billion Pathology market. Proscia’s software platform serves as a central operating layer for digital pathology, supporting clinical and life-sciences customers across the US and Europe. By connecting slide scanners, laboratory information systems, image-analysis applications, AI tools, people, and data, Proscia’s innovative technology enables customers to manage images, data, and workflows in one unified environment. Proscia serves more than 4,000 laboratories, hospitals, and clinics today as well as 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies, with trailing twelve months revenue exceeding $18 million. Proscia was named 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology and earned the highest performance score across both US and European markets.

Agilent and Proscia entered into a multi-year distribution agreement in September 2022 to offer a comprehensive digital diagnostic-pathology system. Today’s announcement builds on Agilent’s established pathology solutions and its partnership with Proscia.

“Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market,” said Agilent president and CEO Padraig McDonnell. “The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use. With Proscia’s leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data. We look forward to welcoming the Proscia team to Agilent and working together to accelerate adoption of AI-enabled pathology workflows to advance drug discovery and companion-diagnostics solutions and create long-term value for customers and shareholders.”

“This agreement with Agilent marks an exciting milestone for Proscia and reflects the strength of the platform our team has built,” said David West, co-founder and CEO of Proscia. “Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions. Together, we can accelerate innovation while continuing to provide customers with the flexibility they need across clinical and life-sciences workflows. I am grateful to the entire Proscia team, whose dedication made this milestone possible, and look forward to building on our work as part of Agilent.”

The combination builds on the successful completion of Agilent’s recent transaction with Biocare Medical, and offers meaningful strategic and financial benefits, including:

• Strengthens Pathology Portfolio with a Leading Digital Pathology Platform. This acquisition strengthens Agilent's existing leadership in pathology instrumentation and reagents, combining industry-leading diagnostic capabilities with Proscia's vendor-agnostic digital pathology platform and established customer base. Proscia’s platform holds FDA 510(k) clearance for primary diagnosis. The transaction builds on Agilent's position as a leader in pathology, well-positioning the Company to address evolving customer needs as the market embraces digitalization and AI.

• Enhances Companion Diagnostics and Biopharma Drug Discovery Offerings. By leveraging a growing repository of real-world data, Proscia offers additional AI-enabled synergies with Agilent's companion diagnostics (CDx) business, enhancing value to biopharma partners as well as clinical and translational research customers.

• Supports Agilent's Long-Term Growth Profile. Proscia’s recurring-revenue model will add a high-growth, high-margin software business to Agilent's pathology portfolio.

The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and is expected to close early in Agilent’s fiscal year 2027. Upon closing, Proscia will become part of the Agilent Life Sciences and Diagnostics Markets Group.

DLA Piper LLP (US) is serving as legal adviser and Joele Frank is serving as strategic communications adviser to Agilent.

Cooley LLP is serving as legal adviser to Proscia.

text:
Jensen Huang told Bloomberg in London he would halt chip supply to a customer building unsafe AI, while saying the current level of concern is not warranted. His prescription is to accelerate containment and monitoring technology, which Nvidia is building a team to sell.

Nvidia’s chief executive says he would stop supplying a customer building unsafe AI. He said it as a hypothetical, then set out the limits.

“It’s a hypothetical, but yes,” Jensen Huang told Bloomberg in London. He would talk to the customer first, he added, because Nvidia does not run other people’s companies and its technology is general-purpose.

The judgement already exists in another form. Nvidia built an approved-buyer list across Singapore, Malaysia and Japan last year, and tighter vetting left more than half its previous customers in the region no longer cleared to buy.

He does not think the worry is warranted. The fears are growing pains, some of the concern is self-imposed, and his remedy is more of the technology: containment and monitoring should be accelerated, because AI is the monitor.

Containment is also a product line. Nvidia has been building a safety team to vet agents before deployment, on the logic that trust, not capability, limits agent adoption.

Wider adoption means more chips. Nvidia profits from the hardware all of it runs on.

He has made the argument before. At Dreamforce last month he said no new laws were needed and that companies should run as fast as they can, pausing only if a product becomes unsafe.

That put him against Dario Amodei, who had called for an industry-wide slowdown with shared standards and an international component.

The safety spending is in Europe this week. Nvidia’s $250M for UK agentic safety research is compute, not cash, with provider selection and commercial terms still to be agreed.

Oxford and University College London are among the institutions that will study safeguards and ways to control AI agents.

Two other executives spent the same day in Europe arguing the other way. Anthropic’s head of international said in Dublin that open models carry more risk by definition, and OpenAI’s finance chief said firms using Chinese models are taking a cybersecurity risk.

Bloomberg puts the reason for asking Huang plainly. Nvidia’s dominance in AI accelerators places it at the centre of the argument over whether the software is slipping out of human control.

description:
Delta Air Lines has officially unveiled its most extensive premium business-class overhaul in nearly three decades, introducing a redesigned Delta One experience featuring upgraded dining, exclusive beverages, enhanced hospitality, and improved sleeping amenities.
The new experience will debut on transoceanic Delta One flights departing Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) this fall, before expanding throughout Delta's global network in early 2027.
The airline's existing premium dining ambitions are already evident at its Los Angeles Delta One Lounge, where personalized restaurant-style service is central to the experience.
The challenge will be delivering comparable consistency across thousands of international flights.

text:
Delta Air Lines has officially unveiled its most extensive premium business-class overhaul in nearly three decades, introducing a redesigned Delta One experience featuring upgraded dining, exclusive beverages, enhanced hospitality, and improved sleeping amenities. While the new experience has been discussed for months, the "new era" was officially announced on Wednesday, representing the airline's latest attempt to establish itself as the leading US carrier for premium international travel, with investments extending well beyond its business-class seats.

The new experience will debut on transoceanic Delta One flights departing Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) this fall, before expanding throughout Delta's global network in early 2027. It comes alongside a wider fleet modernization program exceeding $1 billion, including next-generation Delta One suites on incoming Airbus A350s and redesigned interiors on older A330 aircraft. The airline is also expanding its exclusive lounge network and other premium services.

Delta One Dining Is Getting A Complete Makeover

At the heart of the overhaul is a new culinary program that elevates familiar favorites rather than introducing increasingly elaborate dishes. Working with chefs Simon Hulstone, Norio Ueno, and Jereme Leung, Delta has developed a menu featuring a Wagyu beef burger, roasted sea bass, braised lamb, beef short rib and seasonal risotto. The scale is substantial: Delta produces eight million Delta One meals annually across 50 international kitchens, while its new culinary program incorporates more than 700 ingredients.

Beverages are receiving equally significant attention. Delta is becoming the first airline to serve Blanton's Single Barrel Bourbon, while Dassai 45 sake will be introduced on services to Tokyo Haneda Airport (HND). A redesigned wine program, developed with Master Sommelier Andrea Robinson, includes 13 premium selections from 11 wineries, based on evaluations of more than 1,600 wines. Champagne Taittinger will also expand to domestic Delta One flights, while new Hugo Spritz and Paloma cocktails and mocktails will arrive in 2027.

The improvements also extend to how meals are served. Delta is introducing redesigned tableware, freshly cracked pepper, tableside sauces and an upgraded dessert cart featuring premium sundae toppings and a Champagne sorbet float. The airline's existing premium dining ambitions are already evident at its Los Angeles Delta One Lounge, where personalized restaurant-style service is central to the experience. The challenge will be delivering comparable consistency across thousands of international flights.

Ranjan Goswami, Delta’s chief marketing and product officer, says the changes are grounded in customer insights and the expertise of hundreds of Delta people.

“Our reimagined experience is rooted in solving real customer needs and desires, with intentionality behind every detail. Every investment we make is deliberate and designed to deliver the industry’s most premium end-to-end travel experience. This elevated dining and hospitality experience is about raising the bar while giving customers greater control throughout their journey.”

More Personalized Service & Enhanced Comfort

Beyond dining, Delta is introducing greater flexibility in how passengers structure their flights. Entrées can now be preselected up to 18 hours before departure, six hours closer than before. Expanded options include gluten-free and lighter meals, while travelers prioritizing sleep can skip the full breakfast service in favor of coffee and a croissant before landing. A new "sip and settle" service combines a hot towel, warm nuts, and a preferred beverage without unnecessarily interrupting passengers.

The airline is also refreshing its partnership with Italian fashion house Missoni. New Winter Elsewhere amenity kits will debut on November 3 and include Grown Alchemist skincare, Marvis dental products, and other essentials. A new Missoni Mini pillow will eventually replace the existing cuddle pillow across transoceanic routes, while Bombas socks return on selected flights. These additions build on Delta's earlier investments in Missoni-branded premium amenities and bedding, reflecting the growing importance of sleep quality in business-class competition.

Even after gathering insights from thousands of Delta One customers, Delta conducted extensive internal testing before today's announcement. More than 200 Delta flight attendants and other employees contributed feedback over 14 months, including 36 dedicated trial flights and more than 200 individual submissions. Their recommendations helped shape over 60 new tableware pieces, adjustments to meal presentation and cabin service, and the rollout itself. Rather than introducing everything at once, Delta will roll out the new experience progressively through 2027, allowing crews to adapt to updated procedures.

The Bigger Picture Behind Delta's Premium Transformation

The revamped service is nicely timed with the arrival of Delta's new flagship A350-1000, scheduled to join the fleet in early 2027. Its new Delta One suites will feature lie-flat beds more than three inches longer than current versions, 24-inch entertainment screens, wireless charging, and improved storage. Delta said more than 35,000 engineering hours went into the suite program, involving over 50 suppliers in 15 countries. Meanwhile, older A330-200s and A330-300s will receive suites with privacy doors, helping Delta reach its goal of 90% enclosed Delta One seats by 2030.

The transformation also extends beyond the aircraft. Delta now operates dedicated Delta One Lounges at LAX, John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), while nearly 1,300 aircraft have Delta Sync WiFi. Its ground transportation partnership with Porsche is expanding from 40 to 70 hybrid vehicles across 15 airports and hubs by 2028, although Delta One passengers must book VIP Select for the Porsche service. The investment reinforces the airline's longstanding focus on attracting higher-paying passengers, even as its new Basic Business fares separate onboard luxury from certain ground benefits.

text:
Indianapolis water-conservation advocates support a Boone County utility company’s decision to consider a stream that runs through Lebanon as a water discharge point for the LEAP district instead of Eagle Creek.

Conservationists are worried introducing the water into Eagle Creek, another option for Lebanon Utilities, would kill or drive away the fish and birds that depend on Eagle Creek Reservoir for survival.

“That’s good news for the Eagle Creek Reservoir and good news for Eagle Creek Park,” said Lou Ann Baker, a member of the Eagle Creek Park Advisory Committee.

Lebanon Utilities is looking at Prairie Creek now, which eventually flows into the larger Sugar Creek in west central Indiana. If it’s selected, the utility would build a new treatment plant for the water used by the businesses in the LEAP district and release the treated water into the creek.

The utility is examining how Prairie Creek would be affected by the increased water flow from LEAP district tenants — Meta’s $10 billion hyperscale data center campus and Eli Lilly and Co.’s $4.5 billion Lilly Medicine Foundry.

Lebanon Utilities General Manager Ed Basquill has not responded to Mirror Indy’s request for comment. At a Lebanon Utilities Service Board meeting Sept. 23, Wastewater Operations Manager Ryan Ottinger said the utility commissioned the Boone County Surveyor’s Office to create a report on how discharges from the plant would affect Prairie Creek.

The report by Christopher B. Burke Engineering, LLC looked at how the approximately 1.9 inches more inches of water in the creek would affect Prairie Creek’s flood flows, flood elevation, channel stability and flood storage.

The report is in its draft stage and will receive more input from Indianapolis-based Wessler Engineering and the BF&S Civil Engineers, firms involved with the plant expansion. Lebanon Utilities expects it could take several months to finalize the report.

Alternatives to Eagle Creek Park

Preliminary engineering reports for Lebanon Utilities’ wastewater plant upgrades had identified the location of the water discharge and other treatment structures on a piece of land within Eagle Creek Park between Interstate 65 and Lafayette Road.

But after pushback from Indianapolis officials and community members, Basquill said in a notice released May 1 that “the discharge location will not occur within the limits of Eagle Creek Park.”

Citizens Energy Group, which will provide up to 25 million gallons of water per day to Lebanon Utilities from Indianapolis water sources by 2031, says choosing Prairie Creek would not reduce the amount of water available to Indianapolis.

“While sustainable best practice traditionally favors returning wastewater to its specific watershed of origin — Lebanon Utilities potentially discharging this new volume of wastewater to Prairie Creek would not impair the Central Indiana water resources which provide our water supply, nor would it impair the ability of Citizens Energy Group to provide drinking water for our customers now or in the future,” said Ben Easley, Citizens Energy Group’s corporate and public affairs coordinator.

Baker said she hopes Lebanon Utilities bases its decision on where to place the water discharge on science and data. She also hopes the utility company and other parties involved increase transparency for their decisions and keep the public involved every step of the way.

“You’ve invested millions of dollars in studies, analysis and engineering. Surely you have a plan at this point, and surely you have confidence in that plan to be able to share it with the public,” she said.

What’s next

Lebanon Utilities will have to decide where to discharge the treated water before the treatment plant is built as soon as 2028.

text:
More than three decades later, Smith’s company—now called Axon Enterprise—has sold more than one million Taser devices and diversified its portfolio to include body cameras, drones, and license plate reader cameras to law enforcement, emergency responders, and private-sector security customers.

More recently, Axon has also focused on selling adjacent software and artificial intelligence tools, helping the company report ten consecutive quarters of revenue growth above 30%. But its push into AI coincides with escalating criticism about how officers are using these technologies for surveillance.

Police officers have been either fired or charged with using Flock Safety’s AI-enabled cameras to stalk former romantic partners and other personal connections. AI systems erroneously led to an arrest of a man accused of trying to lure a child from a McDonald’s in 2023, and more recently, led to a Florida woman spending two weeks in jail after being wrongly accused in a deadly hit-and-run incident.

Most of the public’s ire has centered on Flock. Axon has also faced criticism that its AI tools that help officers write police reports make errors, though the company said this occurred during an early access period when agencies could provide feedback before the product’s broader launch. And earlier this month, the Los Angeles City Council voted to delay a pilot program with Axon that would have attached AI-enabled license plate readers on streetlights.

In August, Smith acknowledged that there was a budding anti-surveillance movement that echoed the massive backlash that followed the release of Tasers. “Any new technology in public safety is going to go through an adjustment period, and I would say the critics aren’t all wrong,” Smith told investors during the company’s second-quarter earnings presentation.

Jeff Kunins, who holds the dual roles of chief product officer and chief technology officer at Axon, tells Fortune that the public discourse around surveillance and AI is a complex issue that requires a nuanced conversation.

“I am personally a life-long, die-hard progressive, and I’m here because of that, not in spite of it,” Kunins said. “We view our work as using technology to improve transparency and accountability on both sides…and our role is to build the tech that facilitates public safety.”

When Axon develops new features, Kunins says a third-party independent group, called the Ethics and Equity Advisory Council, makes recommendations during the product design and development process.

He says that when Axon developed Draft One, which utilizes generative AI to take body camera audio and turn it into a first draft of a police report, there were instances where the AI-generated transcript introduced bias based on a subject’s ethnicity. The large language models would generate text that said a white subject “left the scene,” while a Black person “fled the scene,” even when all other factors in the case were identical.

“Obviously, that’s a flagrant example of inappropriate bias coming out of the models solely because of the description of the skin color of the person,” says Kunins. Axon fine-tuned the models to ensure the outputs were more consistent and didn’t introduce harmful bias.

Other AI tools that the company has deployed include Axon Assistant, a tool that can translate more than 50 languages and dialects spoken within the body camera, allowing officers to communicate in the field without needing a human interpreter.

For nearly a decade, Axon has also used AI to help police departments redact data from camera footage, blurring out the faces of bystanders, license plates, and other sensitive details that aren’t involved in an active case. Previously, a law enforcement employee would need to manually go through every frame of a video to obscure those personal details before the footage could be shared with lawyers, the press, and the public.

Internally, Kunins has encouraged collaboration between the engineering team and the broader employee base through hackathon training sessions. The IT department is also tasked with customizing some AI features from software vendors, including Workday and Salesforce, to automate workflows.

There is an even more assertive effort to promote AI usage among Axon’s research and development team, which totals about 2,200 employees. Kunins says that by the end of 2026, Axon expects all work across product management, design, and software engineering to be compressed by 25% to 30%, requiring less labor and organizational capacity than would be needed if the same projects were developed without AI.

To get to that target, Kunins says he’s embraced a carrot and stick approach. Every team has a 10% mandatory target in productivity gains, meaning the baseline requires everyone will have fewer resources to advance new features and products. If teams can show they’ve accelerated those gains by more than 15%, Axon will award them stock grants, as long as the broader team achieves that 10% minimum threshold, according to Kunins.

“We’re expecting to yield about 25%-ish acceleration, not just of the coding part, but of the entire person effort going into these features,” says Kunins.

John Kell

NEWS PACKETS

Meta debuts new AI model. On Monday, Meta announced the roll out of two AI models, called Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, as the social-media giant aims for a stronger foothold in the AI race that had left it trailing well behind rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic. But with the recent debut of the AI agent Meta Muse, and now what it calls its “most capable models” ever launched by the company, CEO Mark Zuckerberg may finally be turning the narrative around on his AI ambitions. The New York Times published a story on how Meta Muse came to fruition, noting that pressure from a tiny startup called Instinct—which had been making its own AI assistants—led Zuckerberg to rush to get Muse out the door even as some top AI leaders within Meta were aware of safety concerns raised during recent tests.

Anthropic’s Claude submits false tip on unsolved homicide case. The latest example of an AI model going rogue involves a case in Philadelphia, where the local police and Anthropic have confirmed that the Claude Haiku 4.5 filled out a tip form reporting it had information about a murder case. While the AI model’s submission was flagged as spam and never probed for investigation, the incident occurred on July 18, but the Philadelphia Police said they weren’t made aware of the incident until Anthropic notified them on October 7. “The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the Philadelphia Police told a local ABC television station.

Microsoft bets on its own AI chips; gives Windows an AI overhaul. Reuters reports on the newest generation of a custom AI chip called Maia 3000 from Microsoft, which can handle coding and complex business tasks. More than a million of these chips are expected to be deployed next year and their predecessor now runs some of Microsoft’s in-house AI models, as well as models from OpenAI. Last week, Microsoft debuted new updates to Windows that incorporate AI agents and other AI tools directly into the company’s PC software. As Fortune reports, one big change involves integrating the Copilot AI app into Windows.

IMF says AI is giving the global economy a boost, but warns of disruption to jobs, taxation. Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, said global growth would remain at around 3% due to strong investments in AI infrastructure while also warning of major disruptions to labor, taxation, and education. She expressed fears that AI will hurt employment by taking over more repetitive tasks from human workers, which could strain government coffers because global economies will favor capital over labor, the latter being a core source of tax income. How much will AI hurt jobs? No one knows, of course, but for every worrying sign—layoffs at major tech giants like Microsoft, HP, and Meta—there’s also data showing that software development job postings have been on the rise.

ADOPTION CURVE

Token bills are looking costly as CIOs struggle to track costs. A new survey of 750 senior executives from companies with annual revenue exceeding $1 billion has found that these businesses collectively spend about $2.5 billion annually on AI tokens, a figure that could increase to close to $3.6 billion within 24 months, according to the research published by professional-services company Accenture. That’s a major ROI challenge as enterprises embrace more agentic AI, given that AI tokens ranked third among cost drivers for the technology, only trailing infrastructure and software development and maintenance.

Accenture says CIOs can get a better grip on costs by embracing more cost-effective, open-weight models and by making every AI-enabled workflow observable before it launches. Other levers involve making every department pay for the AI it uses, automatically routing tasks to the lowest-cost model that can produce the desired outcome, and training employees and developers to understand how to use AI in a cost-effective manner.

Lan Guan, chief AI and data officer, tells Fortune that Accenture’s research concludes that only 20% of enterprise workflows are good candidates for frontier models. CIOs need to be more strategic about building a complex architecture that’s cognizant of token consumption. Yet, Accenture says only 35% of companies can track costs for their largest AI use cases.

“This is not a technical subject anymore; it also involves financial budgeting, behavior changes, and a lot of the cultural changes,” says Guan.

Courtesy of Accenture

text:
Dive Brief:

Johnson & Johnson will leverage “internal strategic investments” to foster growth in its medtech segment, CFO Joseph Wolk said Tuesday during the company’s most recent earnings call.

Those internal investments are “what will propel us to double-digit growth by the end of this decade, in the coming years with increasing performance,” Wolk said in response to an analyst question on whether the pharmaceutical company would be tapping M&A or internal investments as a growth agent. It “does not assume any inorganic additions at this moment in time,” he said.

“We always are on lookout for strategic drivers that could complement our business that makes sense to be in our hands versus where the asset would currently reside, but also creates value for the risk we’re bearing on behalf of shareholders,” Wolk said during the New Brunswick, NJ-based company’s third quarter earnings call, according to a transcript.

Dive Insight:

Sales of the pharma company’s medtech segment inched up by 2.5% for its third quarter, impacted by what Tim Schmid, J&J’s executive VP and worldwide chairman of medtech classed as “temporary headwinds” associated with its Abiomed medical device subsidiary, according to the transcript.

Although results for the segment came in below company expectations, “we are clear on where MedTech performance needs to improve, specifically cardiovascular and surgery outside the U.S. and are taking action to strengthen results,” Wolk said.

“While disappointing, the underlying fundamentals of the MedTech business remain strong,” he said.

Growth in J&J’s “innovative medicine” segment, which includes a range of medications across oncology, immunology and neuroscience, also helped offset the headwinds seen in the medtechs sector, Wolk said on the call.

In a Tuesday post on LinkedIn, Wolk touted the financial impact from J&J’s expanding portfolio, which now includes 29 products or platforms. Together, the portfolio has generated over $1 billion in annual revenue, Wolk, a 28-year company veteran who has served as its CFO for eight years, wrote.

“We are confident in our ability to exceed $100 billion in revenue for the first time in our Company’s 140-year history,” he said, referring to J&J’s updated 2026 full-year guidance which expects estimated reported sales to hit a range between $101 billion to $101.4 billion. “This momentum gives us a clear line of sight to double-digit growth by the end of the decade.”

The pharma company reported an uptick in both sales and operational growth for the quarter ended Sept. 30, with net sales growing by almost 6% to $25 billion, according to its earnings report.

However, the company’s Q3 net earnings of $210 million dropped by nearly 96% year-over-year, impacted by several M&A deals, including its acquisition of Firefly Bio, and the effect of a proposed resolution to litigation that has spanned decades.

Earnings per share of $0.09 for the quarter were impacted by a one-time special charge to its resolution of talc litigation in July, which concerned assertions that certain of its products including talcum powder, such as its baby powder, caused ovarian cancer.

The resolution included a $5.5 billion commitment by J&J to settle 95% of remaining claims after more than a decade of litigation, according to a press release at the time. The first claim payment of $3 billion is set to be made in 2027, with no additional payments due before 2028, J&J said at the time.

The business, which included the $5.5 billion commitment in its GAAP earnings for the quarter under pre-tax adjustments, is currently “trending to meet” that 95% threshold, Wolk said Tuesday.

text:
It's no secret that Microsoft's gaming division has struggled to keep pace with PlayStation and Nintendo for active console users, and this Xbox survey suggests the firm might be considering the nuclear option to fix things.

Yesterday, a new survey appeared for a subset of Xbox users on the Insider Program, presumably among those who Microsoft tracks as having multiple devices. A user sent us the below survey screens, which Windows Central has verified as real.

Microsoft's problematic Xbox multiplatform strategy has left many users who own multiple devices with fewer reasons to actually turn their consoles on. In that universe, it reduces Microsoft's chances to earn users in it's own ecosystem considerably, impacting both first party revenue and third party port viability. Microsoft sells mountains of games on PlayStation, but it has to pay a 30% cut for the privilege. Many PlayStation users already own an Xbox too, so Microsoft is potentially handing away potential users for no real reason.

These new surveys suggest Microsoft may be considering some drastic moves to change the situation.

The survey asks a variety of questions of users across multiple ecosystems, asking how likely they would be to invest in the Xbox platform if various games went timed, or even fully console exclusive.

Microsoft asks if users would switch to Xbox on a per game basis, including pitches of exclusivity for games like Fallout, The Elder Scrolls, DOOM, Hideo Kojima's PHYSINT, Diablo, and even Minecraft itself. The survey even stresses that existing titles wouldn't be removed from other platforms, but would no longer receive new content.

There's even a nuclear option question, asking users how they'd change their habits if every single Xbox game (except Call of Duty, likely owing to acquisition requirements) went fully console exclusive.

It asks users to consider the hypothetical scenario, offering multiple choice responses below it.

"Imagine it was announced that all future title releases from every XBOX-developed gaming franchise except Call of Duty will be console-exclusive to XBOX," the final survey question reads. "For Minecraft only, existing titles would no longer be available for purchase on PlayStation or Nintendo consoles, and would not receive any new content updates. However, there is no impact to any of the existing titles or content you already own. Nothing changes on PC in this announcement."

It asks users if they would move to an existing Xbox console they already own, buy a new one, switch to PC, or skip it entirely in this scenario.

Going multiplatform didn't work, would going maximum exclusivity work instead?

In the near term, even if Microsoft did create massive desire for its platform and was somehow able to make even GTA6 magically exclusive, the RAMpocalypse has driven hardware sales to historic lows. Even if there was Xbox stock available globally, they've become prohibitively expensive for many. But, that situation (hopefully) won't last forever.

If games like Fallout 5, The Elder Scrolls 6, and Diablo 5 were Xbox Helix exclusive, it would undoubtedly drive masses of sales for Xbox hardware. But would the stock even be available? Microsoft has historically struggled with global distribution even before the component crisis. As much as I think Xbox desperately needs exclusive content, the risks are undeniable on paper.

But sacrificing the entire platform is just as risky potentially. PlayStation itself just massively clawed back from Steam and Windows PC gaming too.

There's little point in maintaining Xbox as an entity if it was to become a simple publisher. Microsoft is more of a hardware company than it has ever been arguably, powered by data centers and increasingly home grown silicon, like its new Maia chips which has driven the stock to new highs recently. Microsoft has already sacrificed mobile as a platform endpoint, greatly limiting its ability to distribute and train its AI platforms. I can't imagine they'll seek to make the same mistake with Xbox.

Surveys are just surveys, and it all might amount to nothing. It could also be a hint around Xbox's thought processes. Perhaps there's math that exists that proves that the juice just isn't worth the squeeze. Halo Campaign Evolved on PlayStation likely did irreparable brand damage to Xbox as a hardware entity, even though the game itself wasn't spectacularly well-received.

The future of Xbox could end up being more interesting than expected.

Agilent Technologies has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire digital pathology software developer Proscia in an all-cash transaction valued at $240 million at closing, with up to an additional $30 million tied to future performance milestones.
Proscia provides enterprise software that serves as a central operational platform for digital pathology, connecting slide scanners, laboratory information systems, image-analysis applications, artificial intelligence tools, staff, and data into a unified workflow.
With trailing twelve-month revenue exceeding $18 million, the company was named 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology across both US and European markets.
It also follows Agilent’s recent transaction with Biocare Medical, uniting Agilent’s anatomical pathology instrumentation and staining reagents with Proscia’s open-architecture digital environment.
“Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions.
text:
The all-cash transaction pairs Agilent’s diagnostic instruments and reagents with Proscia’s FDA-cleared, vendor-agnostic software platform.

Agilent Technologies has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire digital pathology software developer Proscia in an all-cash transaction valued at $240 million at closing, with up to an additional $30 million tied to future performance milestones.

The acquisition, which is subject to customary closing conditions, is expected to close early in Agilent’s fiscal year 2027. Following the close, Proscia will join the Agilent Life Sciences and Diagnostics Markets Group.

Proscia provides enterprise software that serves as a central operational platform for digital pathology, connecting slide scanners, laboratory information systems, image-analysis applications, artificial intelligence tools, staff, and data into a unified workflow. The software holds FDA 510(k) clearance for primary diagnosis and is currently utilized by more than 4,000 laboratories, hospitals, and clinics, along with 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies. With trailing twelve-month revenue exceeding $18 million, the company was named 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology across both US and European markets.

“Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market,” says Padraig McDonnell, Agilent president and CEO, in a release. “The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use.

“With Proscia’s leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data. We look forward to welcoming the Proscia team to Agilent and working together to accelerate adoption of AI-enabled pathology workflows to advance drug discovery and companion-diagnostics solutions and create long-term value for customers and shareholders.”

Portfolio Expansion and Companion Diagnostics

The transaction builds on an existing relationship between the companies, which entered into a multi-year commercial distribution agreement in September 2022 to deliver digital diagnostic pathology systems. It also follows Agilent’s recent transaction with Biocare Medical, uniting Agilent’s anatomical pathology instrumentation and staining reagents with Proscia’s open-architecture digital environment.

Beyond routine diagnostic operations, Agilent intends to utilize Proscia’s repository of real-world data to create AI-driven synergies with its companion diagnostics business, targeting applications across translational research and pharmaceutical drug discovery.

“This agreement with Agilent marks an exciting milestone for Proscia and reflects the strength of the platform our team has built,” says David West, co-founder and CEO of Proscia, in a release. “Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions. Together, we can accelerate innovation while continuing to provide customers with the flexibility they need across clinical and life-sciences workflows. I am grateful to the entire Proscia team, whose dedication made this milestone possible, and look forward to building on our work as part of Agilent.”

name: Delta Airlines
title: Delta to offer free in-flight Wi-Fi on all Australian flights within weeks - SMH
description:
A major US carrier has announced that every aircraft on its fleet flying to Australia will offer free in-flight Wi-Fi within the month – and it’s not using Elon Musk’s Starlink services to keep passengers connected.
“The two markets that were the first to have the coverage were Melbourne and Sydney, and over the next three weeks all of our Pacific flying will have the Wi-Fi,” Moomaw said.
Unlike its major US rivals, United, American and Southwest, Delta won’t be using Elon Musk’s Starlink, but its own Delta Sync Wi-Fi, supported by US telco T-Mobile.
Its in-flight Wi-Fi currently relies on satellite services provided by companies such as Viasat.
It may be following a similar strategy to Delta, making sure it gets to control how its customers access Wi-Fi on its flights.
text:
A major US carrier has announced that every aircraft on its fleet flying to Australia will offer free in-flight Wi-Fi within the month – and it’s not using Elon Musk’s Starlink services to keep passengers connected.

Access to fast internet while flying is emerging as a must-have for passengers, particularly on long-haul flights that keep them in the air for stretches of 10 or more hours, and US-based Delta Air Lines is rolling out fast, free Wi-Fi across its trans-Pacific fleet serving Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane.

“We got our final approval from the FCC (US Federal Communications Commission) last week and almost immediately following, we started to roll it out in the Pacific,” Jeff Moomaw, Delta’s vice president Asia Pacific, told this masthead.

Delta flies daily to Sydney year-round, three times a week to Melbourne, increasing to daily by December for peak season. Flights to Brisbane resume at the end of October for three days a week until March 2027.

“The two markets that were the first to have the coverage were Melbourne and Sydney, and over the next three weeks all of our Pacific flying will have the Wi-Fi,” Moomaw said.

Unlike its major US rivals, United, American and Southwest, Delta won’t be using Elon Musk’s Starlink, but its own Delta Sync Wi-Fi, supported by US telco T-Mobile.

Delta’s decision to decline using Starlink sparked a feud with Musk. At the time, he posted on X that the reason Delta declined was because “SpaceX requires that there be no annoying [airline] ‘portal’ to use Starlink”.

Reports have emerged that Delta CEO Ed Bastian said the airline had tested Starlink but didn’t want to proceed with the service.

Bastian reportedly told staff: “We do not want to be with Elon Musk. Trust me.”

Musk responded that Bastian “will lose his job over” his “no” to Starlink.

Download speeds for Starlink range from 25 to 220+ megabits per second, with users sometimes getting more than 100 Mbps: that’s fast enough for movie streaming, gaming, and videoconferencing.

Delta’s Moomaw said the airline’s “no thanks” to Starlink was not driven by a CEO personality clash but rather because of the importance of Wi-Fi to the airline’s DeltaSync ecosystem, which includes in-flight entertainment, connectivity with the app, and new AI functionality.

A 2023 review of Delta Sync put its average download speeds at about 7 Megabits per second with upload rates of 1.3 Mbps – stable but “absolutely unusable for videoconferencing with Zoom and the like”.

Delta is planning to upgrade to high-speed Wi-Fi using Amazon’s LEO on 500 of its aircraft, but it won’t be available until 2028.

Crucially for the airline, LEO can be incorporated into its in-flight entertainment and app ecosystem, and potentially other products, ensuring that Delta maintains its direct relationship with its passengers.

“The difference is we keep it in the ecosystem, which folks like, and that’s why we went with Amazon, because we feel like it’s going to be a better contributor to that ecosystem than just a Wi-Fi provider on its own,” Moomaw said.

Delta’s profitability hinges on premium business and of the four major US airlines, it is the most profitable, helped by its loyalty program partnership with American Express.

The airline has flagged a full-year profit outlook of $US4.5 billion ($6.4 billion), helped by 20 per cent in premium and loyalty revenue growth. Net income in 2025 was $US5.01 billion.

Moomaw says the aviation industry needs to think through its rush to make Musk’s Starlink a standalone supplier of superfast Wi-Fi.

Delta was among the first airlines to announce fast, free Wi-Fi.

“A lot of airlines since then are playing catch-up,” says Moomaw. “And I think one of the easiest ways to do that is that you add a product here or there that’s a bolt-on.”

And that’s how Starlink is acting for airlines. “But it disconnects from the customer and the ecosystem,” Moomaw says.

While the hype around Starlink is growing, reluctance to adopt the Musk model may explain why Qantas, which is famous for long-haul, trans-oceanic travel, is not clamouring for Starlink. Its in-flight Wi-Fi currently relies on satellite services provided by companies such as Viasat. It may be following a similar strategy to Delta, making sure it gets to control how its customers access Wi-Fi on its flights.
